The partial derivative of f with respect to x
practice.why: ∂f/∂x, also written f_x, is the slope when only x changes.
wrong: That is ∂f/∂y. The letter at the bottom tells which input changes.
A value is written f(x, y). ∂f/∂x is a slope.
The curly d signs are not numbers to divide. It means a slope in the x direction.

practice.question: f(x, y) = x² + 4y. What is f(3, 2)?
wrong: You swapped the inputs. In f(3, 2), x = 3 and y = 2.
You took x² as 2 × 3. x² means 3 × 3 = 9.
You added 4 and 2. 4y means 4 × 2.

practice.question: f(x, y) = xy². What is f_x?
practice.why: Treat y as a fixed number. The derivative of x times a number is that number: y².
wrong: That is f_y. For f_x, treat y as fixed and differentiate in x.
You differentiated y as well. For f_x, y² stays as a fixed number.
That adds f_x and f_y. f_x alone is y².

practice.question: At a point, f = 20, f_x = 3 and f_y = 5. You take a small step dx = 0.1 and dy = 0.2. About what is the new value of f?
practice.why: The change is about f_x × dx + f_y × dy = 0.3 + 1 = 1.3, so f is about 21.3.
wrong: That is only the change. Add it to the starting value 20.
You left out the y step. Add f_y × dy = 1 as well.
You added the slopes themselves. Multiply each by its small step first.

entries.concept: second and higher derivatives and the notation f″, f⁽ⁿ⁾, d²y/dx²
entries.evidence: The Maclaurin lesson writes f⁽ⁿ⁾(0) and f″(a) although the skill on second-order derivatives comes later, and nothing before it says what these symbols mean.

screens.title: Differentiating again and again
text: Speed tells how fast your position changes. Acceleration tells how fast your speed changes. So acceleration is a derivative of a derivative.

Differentiate f once and you get f′. Differentiate f′ and you get the second derivative, written f″ ('f double dash') or d²y/dx². It tells how fast the slope itself is changing. Differentiate again for the third derivative, and so on.
Dashes become hard to count, so for the nth derivative we write the number in small brackets: f⁽ⁿ⁾(x) means 'f differentiated n times'. And f⁽ⁿ⁾(0) means: differentiate n times, then put x = 0.
example: Third derivative = 6, and the fourth derivative = 0.

check.question: f(x) = x². What is f″(x)?

practice.question: How is f″ read?
practice.why: f″ has two dashes and is read 'f double dash': the second derivative.
wrong: The dashes are not a power. They count how many times f is differentiated.
That is f′, with one dash. f″ has two.
Nothing is multiplied by 2. Two dashes mean differentiate twice.

practice.question: f(x) = 5x + 1. What is f″(x)?
practice.why: f′(x) = 5, and differentiating the constant 5 gives 0.
wrong: That is f′(x). Differentiate once more.
The constant 1 gives 0 when differentiated. f′ = 5 and f″ = 0.
Differentiating 5x + 1 gives 5, and differentiating again gives 0.

practice.question: f(x) = x³, so f′(x) = 3x² and f″(x) = 6x. What is f″(3)?
wrong: That is f′(3) = 3 × 9. Use the second derivative 6x.
Put x = 3 into 6x. 6 alone is the third derivative.
That is 3². Use f″(x) = 6x.

practice.question: A car's position at time t is f(t) = t². Its speed is f′(t). What is its acceleration f″(t)?
practice.why: f′(t) = 2t, and differentiating 2t gives 2.
wrong: That is the speed f′(t). Differentiate once more for acceleration.
That is the position. Differentiate twice for acceleration.
That is the third derivative. Acceleration is the second: 2.

entries.concept: what a series for a function is (a function written as an endless polynomial) and where its coefficients come from
entries.evidence: The lesson begins 'A Maclaurin series writes f(x) = Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(0) xⁿ/n!' with no word on what it means to write a function as a series or why anyone would.

screens.title: A function as an endless polynomial
text: How does a calculator find e^0.1 or sin 0.1? It cannot look them up. But it is very good at adding and multiplying, and that is all a polynomial needs.

So the idea is to write a hard function as a polynomial that goes on for ever: a + bx + cx² + dx³ + ... Such an endless sum is called a series. The numbers a, b, c, d, ... in front of the powers are its coefficients.

You already know one. The geometric series 1 + x + x² + x³ + ... adds up to 1 ÷ (1 − x) when x is between −1 and 1. So the function 1 ÷ (1 − x) is equal to that series. When x is small, the first few terms already give a very good value.
example: Four terms: 1.111. Each term brings us closer.

check.question: In the series 1 + x + x² + x³ + ..., what is the coefficient of x²?

screens.title: Where the coefficients come from
text: A Maclaurin series is the series of a function in powers of x. Its coefficients come from the derivatives of the function at 0: the coefficient of x to the power n is f⁽ⁿ⁾(0) ÷ n!. Here n! means n × (n − 1) × ... × 2 × 1, so 3! = 6. The sign Σ in the formula only means 'add up all such terms'.

Why does this work? Put x = 0 in the series: only the constant term is left, so it must be f(0). Differentiate once and put x = 0: only the coefficient of x is left, so it is f′(0). Differentiate twice and put x = 0: you get 2 × (coefficient of x²), so that coefficient is f″(0) ÷ 2. Each further step works the same way.
A Taylor series about x = a does the same thing in powers of (x − a), using the derivatives at a instead of at 0. It is the right tool when you care about x near a.
example: f(x) = e^x. Every derivative of e^x is e^x, and e^0 = 1.
So the coefficient of x to the power n is 1 ÷ n!.

check.question: In the Maclaurin series of e^x, what is the coefficient of x²?

practice.question: In a series a + bx + cx² + dx³ + ..., what are the numbers a, b, c, d called?
practice.why: The numbers in front of the powers of x are the coefficients of the series.
wrong: The coefficients come from derivatives, but the numbers in front of the powers are called coefficients.
A factorial is n!. The numbers in front of the powers are coefficients.
The powers are the small numbers on x. The numbers in front are coefficients.

practice.question: Use the first three terms of 1 + x + x² + x³ + ... to estimate 1 ÷ (1 − x) at x = 0.2.
wrong: That uses only two terms. Add x² = 0.04 as well.
You took x² as 2 × 0.2. x² means 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.04.
That is the exact value 1 ÷ 0.8. Three terms give 1.24.

practice.question: In the Maclaurin series of e^x, what is the coefficient of x³?
practice.why: The coefficient of x to the power n is 1 ÷ n!, and 3! = 6.
wrong: Divide by 3!, not by 3. 3! = 6.
Each derivative at 0 is 1, but it must still be divided by 3!.
3! goes underneath: the coefficient is 1 ÷ 6.

practice.question: A function has f(0) = 2, f′(0) = 3 and f″(0) = 8. What is the coefficient of x² in its Maclaurin series?
practice.why: The coefficient of x² is f″(0) ÷ 2! = 8 ÷ 2 = 4.
wrong: f″(0) must be divided by 2! = 2.
That is f′(0), the coefficient of x.
You multiplied by 2. Divide f″(0) by 2!.

entries.concept: the coordinate plane: x-axis, y-axis, origin, and what the two coordinates mean
entries.evidence: The first lesson says 'A point (x, y) is x across from the origin, then y up' without saying what the axes, the origin or coordinates are.

screens.title: Two number lines make a map
text: To tell a friend where you sit in class, you might say 'third column, second row'. Two numbers find the place. A coordinate grid does the same for any point on a flat sheet.

Draw a number line lying flat. It is called the x-axis. Draw a second number line standing straight up through its zero. It is called the y-axis. The point where they cross is called the origin. Both lines read 0 there.
On the x-axis, positive numbers are to the right and negative numbers to the left. On the y-axis, positive numbers are up and negative numbers are down.

Every point gets two numbers in brackets, like (4, 3). They are its coordinates. The first, the x-coordinate, says how far across. The second, the y-coordinate, says how far up or down. The order matters: (4, 3) and (3, 4) are different points.
example: To find (4, 3): start at the origin (0, 0).
Then go 3 up. Mark the point.
(3, 4) is 3 right and 4 up: a different point.

check.question: Start at the origin, go 2 to the right and then 5 up. What are the coordinates of the point you reach?

practice.question: What is the point where the x-axis and the y-axis cross called?
practice.why: The two axes cross at the origin, where both number lines read 0.
wrong: The x-axis is the whole flat number line. The crossing point is the origin.
A coordinate is one of the two numbers of a point. The crossing point is the origin.
The y-axis is the whole upright number line. The crossing point is the origin.

practice.question: Start at the origin, go 5 to the right and then 1 up. What are the coordinates of the point?
practice.why: The first number is how far across (5) and the second is how far up (1).
wrong: The order is swapped. Across comes first, then up.
You went 1 up, so the second number is 1, not 0.
You added the two moves. Write them separately: across, then up.

practice.question: How do you reach the point (−3, 2) from the origin?
practice.why: The x-coordinate −3 means 3 to the left. The y-coordinate 2 means 2 up.
wrong: A negative x-coordinate means go left, not right.
The first number goes with across and it is 3. The second is 2 up.
The first number is across, not down. −3 means 3 to the left.

practice.question: In a hall, a seat at (across, up) tells how far across and how far up it is. Anu sits at (2, 6). Balu sits 3 seats to her right in the same row. Where does Balu sit?
practice.why: Moving right changes only the first number: 2 + 3 = 5. The row stays 6.
wrong: Moving right changes the first number, not the second.
Only the first number changes. The row stays 6.
That is 3 to the left. Right means add: 2 + 3.

entries.concept: why an equation in x and y can be a circle: x² + y² = r² and (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²
entries.evidence: The first lesson starts from 'x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0' and completes the square; that a circle is the set of points at distance r from the centre, and so has such an equation, is only said seven lessons later.

screens.title: A circle as an equation
text: Tie a goat to a post with a 5 metre rope. With the rope pulled tight it walks in a circle: every point of its path is exactly 5 metres from the post. A circle is all the points at one fixed distance, the radius, from one point, the centre.

Put the centre at the origin. By the distance formula, a point (x, y) is √(x² + y²) away from the origin. So it is on the circle of radius r exactly when x² + y² = r². That is the equation of the circle.

If the centre is (h, k) instead, the same idea gives (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². Multiply out the brackets and you get the long 'general' form, with x², y², an x term, a y term and a constant. Completing the square takes you back, so the centre and the radius can be read off.
example: (3, 4): 9 + 16 = 25, so it is on the circle.
(1, 2): 1 + 4 = 5, less than 25, so it is inside.

check.question: What is the radius of the circle x² + y² = 49?

practice.question: A circle is all the points at one fixed distance from one point. What is the fixed distance called?
practice.why: The fixed distance from the centre to every point of the circle is the radius.
wrong: The centre is the fixed point. The fixed distance is the radius.
The origin is the point (0, 0). The fixed distance is the radius.
The equation describes the circle. The fixed distance is the radius.

practice.question: What is the equation of the circle with centre (0, 0) and radius 6?
practice.why: x² + y² = r², and r² = 6² = 36.
wrong: The right side is r², not r: 6² = 36.
You doubled 6. r² means 6 × 6.
That is a straight line. The distance formula squares x and y.

practice.question: What is the centre of the circle (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 16?
practice.why: Compare with (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²: h = 3, and y + 2 = y − (−2), so k = −2.
wrong: The signs are reversed. x − 3 gives h = 3 and y + 2 gives k = −2.
y + 2 means y − (−2), so k = −2.
x − 3 gives h = 3, not −3.

practice.question: A goat is tied to a post at (0, 0) with a 10 metre rope. Which spot is closer than 10 metres to the post?
practice.why: 25 + 64 = 89, which is less than 100, so the spot is inside the circle x² + y² = 100.
wrong: 36 + 64 = 100, so this spot is exactly 10 metres away, on the circle.
81 + 25 = 106, more than 100. Both numbers being under 10 is not enough.
0 + 121 = 121, more than 100. It is 11 metres away.

entries.concept: what an ellipse and a hyperbola are, and their parts (foci, centre, vertices, a, b, c, eccentricity)
entries.evidence: The lesson 'Eccentricity of an ellipse or a hyperbola' uses e = c/a, foci, semi-axis and c² = a² ∓ b² straight away; no lesson says what an ellipse or a hyperbola is.

screens.title: The ellipse: an oval from two pins
text: Push two pins into a board. Lay a loose loop of string round them, pull it tight with a pencil, and move the pencil all the way round. You draw an oval called an ellipse. The string does not change length, so for every point on the curve, (distance to one pin) + (distance to the other pin) is the same.

Each pin is a focus (plural: foci). The point midway between the foci is the centre. The longest width, through the foci, is the major axis, and half of it is called a. The shortest width is the minor axis, and half of it is b. The ends of the major axis are the vertices. The distance from the centre to a focus is c.
With the centre at the origin and the foci on the x-axis, the equation is x²/a² + y²/b² = 1, and c² = a² − b². The fixed sum of the two distances is 2a.
example: x²/25 + y²/9 = 1, so a = 5 and b = 3.
c² = 25 − 9 = 16, so c = 4. The foci are (4, 0) and (−4, 0).

check.question: For the ellipse x²/25 + y²/9 = 1, how long is the major axis?

screens.title: The hyperbola: two branches
text: Look at the edge of the light that a table lamp with a round shade throws on the wall. That curve is a hyperbola. It comes from keeping the difference of the two distances to the foci fixed, instead of their sum. The result is two separate branches that open away from each other.

There are still two foci, and a centre midway between them. The two points where the curve crosses the line through the foci are the vertices. The distance from the centre to a vertex is a, and the segment joining the vertices is the transverse axis, of length 2a. The distance from the centre to a focus is c. Now c is bigger than a.
With the centre at the origin and the foci on the x-axis, the equation is x²/a² − y²/b² = 1, and c² = a² + b². The fixed difference of the distances is 2a.
The eccentricity e = c ÷ a says how far a curve is from being a circle. For a circle it is 0, for an ellipse it is between 0 and 1, and for a hyperbola it is more than 1.
example: x²/9 − y²/16 = 1, so a = 3 and b = 4.
c² = 9 + 16 = 25, so c = 5. The foci are (5, 0) and (−5, 0).
e = c ÷ a = 5 ÷ 3, which is more than 1.

check.question: An ellipse has a = 5 and c = 4. What is its eccentricity?

practice.question: An ellipse is drawn with a loop of string round two pins. What is each pin called?
practice.why: Each pin is a focus. The two together are the foci.
wrong: The vertices are the ends of the major axis, on the curve itself.
The centre is the point midway between the two pins.
An axis is a width of the ellipse, not a point.

practice.question: For the ellipse x²/100 + y²/36 = 1, what is c?
practice.why: For an ellipse c² = a² − b² = 100 − 36 = 64, so c = 8.
wrong: That is c². Take the square root.
You added. For an ellipse c² = a² − b².
That is a − b = 10 − 6. Use c² = a² − b².

practice.question: For the hyperbola x²/16 − y²/9 = 1, what is c?
practice.why: For a hyperbola c² = a² + b² = 16 + 9 = 25, so c = 5.
wrong: That uses the ellipse rule a² − b². For a hyperbola c² = a² + b².
That is c². Take the square root.
That is a + b = 4 + 3. Use c² = a² + b².

practice.question: A curve has a = 4 and c = 5. What kind of curve is it?
practice.why: e = c ÷ a = 5 ÷ 4 = 1.25, which is more than 1, so it is a hyperbola.
wrong: You did a ÷ c. The eccentricity is c ÷ a = 1.25.
e is right, but an ellipse has e between 0 and 1.

entries.concept: the absolute value bars | |
entries.evidence: The area formula 'Area = ½ |x₁(y₂ − y₃) + ...|' and the step '½ × |−10| = 5' use the bars, but absolute value is only taught in a class 11 skill.

screens.title: The bars mean size only
text: A lift standing 3 floors below the ground is at floor −3. How far is it from the ground floor? 3 floors. A distance does not care about direction.
The absolute value of a number is its distance from 0 on the number line. It is written with two upright bars: |−3| = 3 and |3| = 3. It removes a minus sign and leaves a positive number as it is.
An area can never be negative. But a formula built from coordinates can come out negative, depending on the order in which you take the points. The bars put that right.

check.question: What is |−7|?

practice.question: What is the absolute value of a number?
options: The number with a minus sign put on
The number with its sign changed
practice.why: The absolute value is how far the number is from 0 on the number line.
wrong: The bars remove a minus sign. They never add one.
The bars do not square. They give the distance from 0.
A positive number stays as it is. Only a minus sign is removed.

practice.question: What is |−12|?
practice.why: −12 is 12 steps from 0, so |−12| = 12.
wrong: The bars remove the minus sign. A distance is not negative.
0 is where the distance is measured from. −12 is 12 steps away.
The bars do not turn the number over. They give the distance from 0.

practice.question: Which statement is true?
practice.why: −6 and 6 are both 6 steps from 0, so both bars give 6.
wrong: An absolute value is never negative. |−6| = 6.
−6 is less than 5, but its size 6 is more than 5.
The bars leave a positive number as it is. |6| = 6.

practice.question: A formula for the area of a triangle gives ½ × |−18|. What is the area?
wrong: The bars remove the minus sign first. An area cannot be negative.
You forgot the ½. Half of 18 is 9.
The bars remove the minus sign, and then you halve: ½ × 18.

entries.concept: three coordinates (x, y, z) for a point in space, and the z-axis
entries.evidence: The first lesson finds the distance between P(4, −2, 0) and Q(1, −5, −3) 'across the floor (x and y) and then up (z)' without any lesson saying what a third coordinate or the z-axis is.

screens.title: A third number for height
text: A fly is somewhere in your room. Saying '2 metres from this wall and 3 metres from that wall' fixes only a spot on the floor. The fly may be above it. You need a third number: its height.

In space we use three axes that meet at the origin, each at right angles to the other two. Think of a corner of the room: the x-axis and the y-axis run along the floor, and the z-axis runs straight up.

A point is written (x, y, z). To reach it from the origin, go x along the x-axis, then y in the direction of the y-axis, then z straight up (or down if z is negative). Points on the floor have z = 0, so (2, 3, 0) is the floor point directly below (2, 3, 4).
example: To reach (2, 3, 4): go 2 along x, 3 along y, then 4 up.
Distance from the origin, in two steps:

check.question: How high above the floor (the plane z = 0) is the point (5, 1, 7)?

practice.question: In the point (x, y, z), which number gives the height above the floor?
practice.why: The z-axis runs straight up, so z is the height above the floor z = 0.
wrong: x is a distance along the floor, not up; height is z.
y is a distance along the floor, not up; height is z.
Adding x and y still stays on the floor; height is the third number z.

practice.question: Which floor point (z = 0) lies directly below (4, 1, 6)?
practice.why: Directly below keeps x and y the same and makes z = 0, giving (4, 1, 0).
wrong: You kept the height and dropped x and y; keep x and y and set z to 0.
You set y to 0 instead of z; the floor is z = 0.
You set x to 0 instead of z; the floor is z = 0.

practice.question: How far is the point (1, 2, 2) from the origin?
wrong: You added the coordinates; add their squares and then take the square root.
You stopped at 9; the distance is the square root of 9.
You left out z; after the floor step 1² + 2² = 5, add 2² as well.

practice.question: A point is at (2, 5, −3). Where is it compared with the floor z = 0?
practice.why: z = −3, and a negative z means go down, so the point is 3 below the floor.
wrong: You ignored the minus sign; a negative z means down.
You read x; the height comes from z, which is −3.
You read y; the height comes from z, which is −3.

entries.concept: the vector equation of a line r = a + λb (a point plus multiples of a direction), the parameter λ, direction ratios
entries.evidence: The lesson 'Parallel, intersecting or skew lines' gives lines as r⃗ = (…) + λ(…) and the first worked example says 'Direction ratios: B − A', before the form is explained four lessons later; direction ratios are never defined.

screens.title: A line is a start point plus steps
text: To describe a straight road, you can name one place on it and say which way it runs. A line in space is described the same way.

Let a be the position vector of one known point of the line, and let b be a vector that points along the line. Start at a and add any amount of b: r = a + λb. Here λ (the Greek letter lambda) is any number, positive, negative or a fraction. It is called a parameter. Each value of λ gives one point of the line, and every point of the line comes from some λ. A second line usually uses another letter, μ (mu).

The three components of b are called direction ratios of the line. Any multiple of b points along the same line, so (1, 2, 3) and (2, 4, 6) are direction ratios of the same direction. Divide them by the length of b and you get the direction cosines.

check.question: On the line r = (1, 0, 2) + λ(2, 1, −1), which point has λ = 2?

practice.question: In r = a + λb, what is λ called?
practice.why: λ is the number that changes; each value gives one point of the line. It is called a parameter.
wrong: Direction ratios are the components of b, not λ.
The position vector of the known point is a, not λ.
Direction cosines come from dividing b by its length; λ is the parameter.

practice.question: On the line r = (2, 1, 0) + λ(1, 3, 2), which point has λ = 2?
wrong: You used λ = 1; multiply the direction by 2.
You forgot to add the start point (2, 1, 0).
You doubled the start point instead of the direction; λ multiplies b.

practice.question: A line has direction ratios (1, −2, 3). Which of these are also direction ratios of the same line?
practice.why: Any multiple of b points along the same line, and 3 × (1, −2, 3) = (3, −6, 9).
wrong: You added 1 to each number; only multiplying keeps the direction.
You dropped the minus sign, which changes the direction.
You reversed the order of the numbers, which gives another direction.

practice.question: On the line r = (3, 0, 1) + λ(1, 1, −2), which value of λ gives the point (1, −2, 5)?
wrong: λ = 2 gives (5, 2, −3); the sign is wrong, so step backwards.
λ = −1 gives (2, −1, 3); one more backward step is needed.
λ = 1 gives (4, 1, −1); the point lies in the backward direction.

entries.concept: what the equation of a plane ax + by + cz + d = 0 is, and its normal (a, b, c)
entries.evidence: The first lesson measures a distance to 'the plane 2x + 2y − z + 1 = 0' 'along the normal (a, b, c)' before anything says that such an equation is a plane or why (a, b, c) is perpendicular to it.

screens.title: A flat surface and its normal
text: A table top is part of a plane: a flat surface that goes on for ever in every direction. A table leg stands at right angles to it. A direction at right angles to a plane is called its normal.

In space, one equation in x, y and z describes a surface, not a line. The simplest are flat: z = 0 is the floor, and z = 3 is a flat ceiling 3 units up. In general a plane has an equation ax + by + cz + d = 0. A point is on the plane exactly when its coordinates fit the equation.
The numbers in front of x, y and z make a normal vector of the plane: (a, b, c) is at right angles to it. That is why these three numbers appear in the formulas for distances and angles.
example: (1, 1, 2): 4 − 3 = 1, not 0, so it is off the plane.
A step inside the plane, from (3, 0, 0) to (0, 3, 0), is (−3, 3, 0).
Dot it with the normal (1, 1, 1): −3 + 3 + 0 = 0. At right angles.

check.question: Is the point (1, 2, 0) on the plane x + y + z − 3 = 0?

practice.question: A direction at right angles to a plane is called its
practice.why: Like a table leg standing at right angles to the table top, this direction is the normal.
wrong: The origin is a point where the axes meet, not a direction at right angles to a plane.
An axis is a reference line; the direction at right angles to a plane is its normal.
Slope measures steepness of a line; the word here is normal.

practice.question: What is a normal vector of the plane 2x − y + 5z + 7 = 0?
practice.why: The numbers in front of x, y and z are 2, −1 and 5, so the normal is (2, −1, 5).
wrong: You dropped the minus sign in front of y.
You used d = 7; the normal uses only the numbers in front of x, y and z.
You skipped the y number and used d; take a, b, c only.

practice.question: Which point is on the plane x + 2y + z − 6 = 0?
practice.why: 1 + 2 × 2 + 1 − 6 = 0, so (1, 2, 1) fits the equation.
wrong: You forgot to double y: 2 + 4 + 2 − 6 = 2, not 0.
You used d as a coordinate: 0 + 0 − 6 − 6 = −12, not 0.
1 + 4 + 3 − 6 = 2, not 0; put the point in and check that you get 0.

practice.question: A flat ceiling is 4 units above the floor z = 0. What is its equation?
practice.why: Every point of the ceiling has height 4, so its equation is z = 4.
wrong: x = 4 is an upright wall; height is given by z.
z = 0 is the floor itself, not the ceiling.
That plane is tilted: it contains the floor point (4, 0, 0). A flat ceiling needs only z = 4.

entries.concept: what slope measures (rise ÷ run) and what the equation of a line y = mx + c means
entries.evidence: The first lesson says 'A straight line has the same slope everywhere' and uses m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) and y = mx + c, but no lesson says what slope measures or why such an equation is a line.

screens.title: Slope: how steep?
text: A ramp that rises 1 metre for every 2 metres forward is gentle. A ramp that rises 3 metres for every 2 metres forward is steep. We measure steepness by rise ÷ run.

For a line on a grid, pick any two points on it. The rise is the change in y. The run is the change in x. The slope is rise ÷ run, and its letter is m. On a straight line you get the same answer whichever two points you pick. That is what makes it straight.

A line going uphill from left to right has a positive slope. Downhill is negative. A flat line has slope 0. A line going straight up and down has no slope, because its run is 0 and we cannot divide by 0.
example: Slope = 6 ÷ 2 = 3: for every 1 step right, the line goes 3 up.

check.question: A line passes through (0, 0) and (2, 4). What is its slope?

screens.title: An equation that draws a line
text: Take the rule y = 2x + 1. For x = 0, 1, 2 it gives y = 1, 3, 5. Plot (0, 1), (1, 3) and (2, 5): they lie on one straight line.
The equation of a line is a rule that is true for every point on the line and for no other point. To test a point, put its x and y into the equation.

In y = mx + c, the number m is the slope. The number c is where the line crosses the y-axis, because x = 0 gives y = c. It is called the y-intercept. So to write the equation of a line you need two things: its slope, and one point to fix c.
example: From (0, 1) to (1, 3): rise 2, run 1, so the slope is 2. That is m.
It crosses the y-axis at (0, 1), so c = 1.

check.question: What is the slope of the line y = 5x − 2?

practice.question: Which of these gives the slope of a line?
practice.why: Steepness is measured by rise ÷ run: change in y divided by change in x.
wrong: You turned the fraction upside down; rise goes on top.
Slope divides rise by run; it does not multiply them.
Slope divides rise by run; it does not subtract them.

practice.question: A line passes through (1, 3) and (4, 9). What is its slope?
practice.why: Rise = 9 − 3 = 6 and run = 4 − 1 = 3, so slope = 6 ÷ 3 = 2.
wrong: You did run ÷ rise; slope is rise ÷ run.
3 is only the run; divide the rise 6 by it.
6 is only the rise; divide it by the run 3.

practice.question: Where does the line y = 3x − 4 cross the y-axis?
practice.why: Put x = 0: y = 3 × 0 − 4 = −4. So c = −4 is the y-intercept.
wrong: 3 is the slope m; the crossing point is c.
You dropped the minus sign; c is −4.
You put x = 1; the y-axis is where x = 0.

practice.question: A ramp rises 2 metres for every 8 metres forward. What is its slope?
practice.why: Slope = rise ÷ run = 2 ÷ 8 = 1/4.
wrong: You did run ÷ rise; rise goes on top.
You multiplied; slope is rise ÷ run.
You subtracted; slope is rise ÷ run.

entries.concept: what a protractor is and how to place it
entries.evidence: The first lesson begins 'A protractor has two scales running in opposite directions' without saying what a protractor is, where its centre is, or how it is laid on an angle.

screens.title: Meet the protractor
text: A ruler measures length. A protractor measures angles. It is a flat half circle, usually of clear plastic.

Along its curved edge are marks from 0 to 180. Each small step is 1 degree. In the middle of its straight edge is a small mark called the centre. The line through the centre along the straight edge is the zero line.

To measure an angle, put the centre exactly on the corner of the angle. Turn the protractor until the zero line lies along one arm. Then read the number where the other arm crosses the curved edge. There are two rows of numbers so that you can start from the left or from the right. Use the row that shows 0 on your first arm.
example: One arm lies on the 0 of the inner row.
The other arm crosses the mark 60 on the inner row.
The outer row says 120 there. We do not use it, because the outer row does not show 0 on the first arm.

check.question: The first arm is on 0 and the other arm is on 90 of the same row. How big is the angle?

practice.question: Which tool measures angles?
practice.why: A protractor is the half circle marked from 0 to 180 that measures angles.
wrong: A ruler measures length, not angles.
A tape measures length, not angles.
Scissors make an angle when opened, but they do not measure it.

practice.question: Where do you put the centre of the protractor?
options: On the corner of the angle
On the end of one arm
In the middle of one arm
practice.why: The centre mark must sit exactly on the corner of the angle.
wrong: The end of an arm is not the corner; the centre goes where the two arms meet.
The centre goes where the two arms meet, not part of the way along an arm.
It must be exactly on the corner, or the reading will be wrong.

practice.question: The first arm is on 0 of the outer row. The other arm crosses a mark where the outer row says 50 and the inner row says 130. How big is the angle?
practice.why: Use the row that shows 0 on the first arm. That is the outer row, which says 50.
wrong: You read the inner row; use the row that shows 0 on the first arm.
You added the two rows; read only the row that starts at 0 on the first arm.
You subtracted the two rows; read only the outer row.

practice.question: How big is each small step on the curved edge of a protractor?
practice.why: The marks go from 0 to 180 and each small step is 1 degree.
wrong: The numbers are often printed every 10, but each small step is 1 degree.
Centimetres measure length; a protractor's steps are degrees.
180 is the whole curved edge, not one step.

entries.concept: what an angle is, and what a degree (the sign °) means
entries.evidence: The first lesson opens with 'A right angle (90°) is a square corner' before any lesson has said what an angle is or what the sign ° measures.

screens.title: What is an angle?
text: Open a pair of scissors a little. Now open them wide. The two blades start from the same point, and the opening between them changes.
When two straight lines start from one point, the opening between them is called an angle. The angle tells how far one line has turned away from the other.
The size of an angle does not depend on how long the lines are. Long scissors and short scissors opened the same amount make the same angle.
example: Open it a little: a small angle between the covers.
Open it wider: a bigger angle.
Lay it flat: the covers make one straight line.

check.question: Which makes the bigger angle: scissors opened wide, or scissors opened a little?

screens.title: Measuring a turn in degrees
text: We measure length in centimetres. We measure turn in degrees. The sign for degrees is a small raised circle: 90° is read as 90 degrees.
Think of one full turn, all the way round. People agreed to cut it into 360 equal tiny turns. Each tiny turn is 1 degree. So a full turn is 360°.
A half turn is 180°. It makes a straight line. A quarter turn is 90°. It makes a square corner, and it is called a right angle.
example: The corner of a page is a quarter turn, so it is 90°.

check.question: How many degrees is a right angle?

practice.question: Two straight lines start from one point. The opening between them is called
practice.why: The opening between two lines that start from one point is an angle.
wrong: A degree is the unit we measure with; the opening itself is an angle.
The lines make the opening; the opening is called an angle.
A full turn is one special size, 360°; any opening is called an angle.

practice.question: How many degrees is a half turn?
practice.why: A full turn is 360°, and 360° ÷ 2 = 180°.
wrong: 90° is a quarter turn; a half turn is 360° ÷ 2.
360° is a full turn; halve it.
You halved a quarter turn; halve the full turn, 360°.

practice.question: Long scissors and short scissors are opened the same amount. Which makes the bigger angle?
practice.why: The size of an angle does not depend on how long the lines are, only on the opening.
wrong: Longer blades do not make a bigger angle; only the opening counts.
Shorter blades do not make a bigger angle; only the opening counts.
We can tell: the same opening gives the same angle.

practice.question: You make three quarter turns. How many degrees is that?
practice.why: One quarter turn is 90°, and 90° × 3 = 270°.
wrong: 180° is two quarter turns; count three.
360° is four quarter turns, a full turn.
You added 3 to 90; take 90° three times.

entries.concept: cevian, and the ratio in which a point divides a side
entries.evidence: The lessons multiply 'the three ratios (BD/DC)(CE/EA)(AF/FB)' and speak of 'the cevians' meeting, without saying what a cevian is or what BD/DC measures.

screens.title: Cevians and the parts of a side
text: Tie a string from one corner of a triangular frame to any point on the opposite side. A segment like this, from a corner to a point on the opposite side, is called a cevian (after the mathematician Ceva). Medians, altitudes and angle bisectors are all cevians.
The point D where a cevian from A lands on BC cuts BC into two parts, BD and DC. The ratio BD : DC compares them, and BD/DC is the same ratio written as a fraction.

In the same way, let the cevian from B land at E on CA, and the cevian from C land at F on AB. Go round the triangle one way: B to C, C to A, A to B. That gives three ratios: BD/DC, CE/EA and AF/FB. Ceva's theorem says three cevians pass through one point exactly when these three multiply to 1.
example: Take the three medians: D, E and F are midpoints.
BD = DC, so BD/DC = 1. In the same way CE/EA = 1 and AF/FB = 1.
1 × 1 × 1 = 1, so the three medians meet at one point.

check.question: D is on BC with BD = 2 cm and DC = 6 cm. What is BD : DC in simplest form?

practice.question: A segment from a corner of a triangle to a point on the opposite side is called
practice.why: Any segment from a corner to a point on the opposite side is a cevian.
wrong: A ratio compares two lengths; the segment itself is a cevian.
A side joins two corners; a cevian goes from a corner to the opposite side.
A midpoint is a point, not a segment.

practice.question: D is on BC with BD = 4 cm and DC = 10 cm. What is BD : DC in simplest form?
practice.why: BD : DC = 4 : 10. Divide both by 2 to get 2 : 5.
wrong: You wrote DC first; the order is BD then DC.
You compared BD with the whole side BC; compare BD with DC.
You compared BD with the whole side BC (4 : 14); compare BD with DC.

practice.question: BC = 12 cm and D is on BC with BD = 3 cm. What is BD : DC?
wrong: You used the whole side BC; first find DC = 12 − 3 = 9.
You wrote DC first; the order is BD then DC.
You compared BC with BD; find DC = 9 and compare BD with it.

practice.question: Three cevians have BD/DC = 2 and CE/EA = 3. What must AF/FB be for them to pass through one point?
practice.why: The three ratios must multiply to 1: 2 × 3 × AF/FB = 1, so AF/FB = 1/6.
wrong: You multiplied 2 × 3; the product of all three must be 1, so the third is 1/6.
You added the ratios; they are multiplied, and the product must be 1.
Each ratio need not be 1; only their product must be 1.

entries.concept: tangent, point of contact and secant
entries.evidence: The first lesson starts 'A tangent meets the radius at the point of contact at a right angle' and asks for 'the length of the tangent from P'; what a tangent is appears only in the fourth lesson.

screens.title: A line that just touches
text: Look at a bicycle wheel standing on a flat road. The road touches the wheel at just one point. A straight line that touches a circle at exactly one point is called a tangent. That one point is the point of contact.

A line that cuts through a circle meets it at two points; it is called a secant. From a point P outside the circle you can draw two tangents. 'The length of the tangent from P' means the distance from P to the point of contact T.

The spoke that goes straight down to the road is upright. In the same way, the radius drawn to the point of contact always meets the tangent at a right angle. This gives a right-angled triangle to work with.
example: Centre O, radius OT = 3 cm, and P is outside with OP = 5 cm.
Triangle OTP has its right angle at T, so OP is the longest side.

check.question: At how many points does a tangent meet a circle?

practice.question: A line that cuts a circle at two points is called
practice.why: A line meeting the circle at two points is a secant.
wrong: A tangent touches the circle at exactly one point.
A radius goes from the centre to the circle; it is not a line cutting through.
The point of contact is where a tangent touches, not a line.

practice.question: At what angle does the radius drawn to the point of contact meet the tangent?
practice.why: The radius to the point of contact always meets the tangent at a right angle, 90°.
wrong: 180° would make them one straight line; they meet at a right angle.
The angle is always a right angle, 90°, not half of it.
The angle does not vary; it is always 90°.

practice.question: O is the centre, the radius OT = 6 cm, and PT is a tangent with OP = 10 cm. How long is PT?
practice.why: The right angle is at T, so PT² = 10² − 6² = 100 − 36 = 64 and PT = 8 cm.
wrong: You subtracted the lengths; subtract their squares and take the root.
You added the lengths; use PT² = OP² − OT².
You added the squares; OP is the longest side, so subtract 6² from 10².

practice.question: PT is a tangent of length 12 cm and the radius OT = 5 cm. How far is P from the centre O?
practice.why: The right angle is at T, so OP² = 12² + 5² = 144 + 25 = 169 and OP = 13 cm.
wrong: You added the lengths; add their squares and take the root.
You subtracted the lengths; add the squares, since OP is the longest side.
You subtracted the squares; OP is the longest side, so add them.

entries.concept: the angle an arc makes (subtends) at the centre and on the circle; segment; cyclic quadrilateral
entries.evidence: The first lesson says 'An arc makes twice the angle at the centre that it makes at any point on the rest of the circle ... angles in the same segment ... cyclic quadrilateral' with none of these ideas set up (the parts of a circle come three lessons later).

screens.title: The angle an arc makes
text: Sit in a round stadium and look at the two goalposts A and B. The opening between your two lines of sight is an angle. It is the angle that AB makes at your seat.

Take an arc AB of a circle with centre O. Join A and B to O: angle AOB is the angle the arc makes at the centre. Now pick a point C on the rest of the circle and join A and B to C: angle ACB is the angle the arc makes at a point on the circle. Books say the arc 'subtends' these angles; it only means 'makes'.
The key fact of this skill: the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circle on the same arc.
example: Arc AB makes angle AOB = 100° at the centre.
At a point C on the rest of the circle, angle ACB = 100° ÷ 2 = 50°.
At another such point D, angle ADB = 50° as well.
If AB is a diameter, angle AOB = 180°, so angle ACB = 90°.

check.question: The angle at the centre is 80°. What is the angle at a point on the circle, on the same arc?

screens.title: Segments and cyclic quadrilaterals
text: A chord is a straight line joining two points of a circle. A chord AB cuts the inside of the circle into two pieces. Each piece is called a segment. A diameter cuts it into two equal segments, called semicircles.
'Angles in the same segment' are angles such as ACB and ADB, where C and D are on the circle on the same side of the chord AB. They stand on the same arc, so they are equal.
A quadrilateral with all four corners on one circle is called a cyclic quadrilateral. Points that lie on one circle are called concyclic. In a cyclic quadrilateral, opposite angles add up to 180°.
example: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with angle A = 70°.
Angle C is opposite angle A.

check.question: Where do the four corners of a cyclic quadrilateral lie?

practice.question: A quadrilateral with all four corners on one circle is called
practice.why: Four corners on one circle make a cyclic quadrilateral.
wrong: A segment is a piece of the circle cut off by a chord.
A semicircle is half a circle, cut by a diameter.
A chord is a straight line joining two points of a circle.

practice.question: An arc makes an angle of 35° at a point on the circle. What angle does it make at the centre?
practice.why: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circle: 2 × 35° = 70°.
wrong: You halved; the centre angle is the bigger one, twice 35°.
The two angles are not equal; the centre angle is double.
You took it from 180°; that rule is for opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral.

practice.question: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with angle B = 85°. What is angle D?
practice.why: D is opposite B, and opposite angles add up to 180°: 180° − 85° = 95°.
wrong: Opposite angles are not equal; they add up to 180°.
You took it from 360°; opposite angles add up to 180°.
You took it from 90°; opposite angles add up to 180°.

practice.question: C and D are on a circle, on the same side of the chord AB. Angle ACB = 40°. What is angle ADB?
practice.why: Angles in the same segment stand on the same arc, so they are equal: 40°.
wrong: Doubling gives the angle at the centre, but D is on the circle.
Halving is not needed; both angles are on the circle, so they are equal.
180° − 40° is for opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral; these are in the same segment.

entries.concept: compasses, centre, radius and arc in a construction
entries.evidence: The first worked construction says 'With centres A and B and radius r > 3 cm, draw arcs' although the skill that explains what compasses do comes after this one.

screens.title: What compasses draw
text: Compasses have two legs: one with a sharp point and one with a pencil. Once you open them, the gap between the point and the pencil stays the same.

Press the point on the paper at a place P and swing the pencil round. You get a circle. If you swing only part of the way, you get a piece of a circle, called an arc. P is the centre. The gap you chose is the radius.
Every point of the arc is the same distance from the centre. So 'with centre A and radius 4 cm, draw an arc' means: open the compasses to 4 cm on a ruler, put the point on A, and draw a curve.
example: Open the compasses to 4 cm. Draw an arc with centre A.
Keep the same opening. Draw an arc with centre B.
The arcs cross at P. P is on both arcs.
So PA = 4 cm and PB = 4 cm: PA = PB.

check.question: An arc is drawn with centre A and radius 5 cm. How far from A is any point on the arc?

practice.question: A piece of a circle drawn with compasses is called
practice.why: Swinging the pencil only part of the way round gives a piece of a circle, called an arc.
wrong: The radius is the opening of the compasses, not the curve.
The centre is where the sharp point stands.
The gap is the opening between point and pencil; the curve is an arc.

practice.question: An arc is drawn with centre B and radius 7 cm. P is a point on the arc. How long is PB?
practice.why: Every point of the arc is the same distance from the centre, the radius 7 cm.
wrong: You doubled the radius; the distance from the centre is the radius itself.
You halved the radius; the distance from the centre is the radius itself.
We can tell: every point of the arc is 7 cm from B.

practice.question: An arc with centre A and radius 3 cm crosses an arc with centre B and radius 5 cm at P. Which is true?
practice.why: P is on both arcs, so it is 3 cm from A and 5 cm from B.
wrong: PA = PB only when both arcs use the same opening; here they are 3 cm and 5 cm.
You swapped them; the arc with centre A has radius 3 cm.
Adding the radii does not give AB; the arcs only tell us PA and PB.

practice.question: A goat is tied to a post with a 6 m rope. It walks round with the rope tight. What is the post?
practice.why: The goat stays 6 m from the post all the time, so the post is the centre.
wrong: The rope, 6 m, is the radius; the post is the centre.
Part of the goat's path is an arc; the post is the centre.
The goat's path is the circle; the post is its centre.

entries.concept: bisect, midpoint, perpendicular bisector and angle bisector
entries.evidence: The lesson defines the perpendicular bisector only as 'the set of all points the same distance from A and from B' and never says that to bisect is to cut into two equal parts.

screens.title: Cutting exactly in half
text: Fold a strip of paper so that its two ends meet. The fold cuts the strip into two equal parts. To bisect something means to cut it into two equal parts.
The point that cuts a line segment AB into two equal parts is its midpoint M, so AM = MB. The perpendicular bisector of AB is the line through M that crosses AB at a right angle (90°).
An angle can be bisected too. The angle bisector is the line from the corner of the angle that cuts it into two equal angles.
example: AB = 6 cm. Its midpoint M is 3 cm from A and 3 cm from B.
The line through M at 90° to AB is the perpendicular bisector of AB.
An angle of 80° is bisected into two angles of 40°.

check.question: An angle of 60° is bisected. How big is each part?

practice.question: To bisect something means to cut it into
practice.why: Bisect means cut into two equal parts, like a fold that makes the ends meet.
wrong: The two parts must be equal.
Bisect means two parts, not three.
Bisect means two parts, not four.

practice.question: AB = 10 cm and M is its midpoint. How long is AM?
practice.why: The midpoint cuts AB into two equal parts: 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm.
wrong: That is the whole segment; AM is half of it.
You doubled; the midpoint halves the segment.
You halved twice; halve only once.

practice.question: A line crosses AB at its midpoint, at an angle of 60°. Is it the perpendicular bisector of AB?
options: Yes, because it passes through the midpoint
Yes, any line that crosses AB is one
No, it must pass through A
No, it must cross AB at 90°
practice.why: A perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint and crosses at a right angle, 90°. This one crosses at 60°.
wrong: The midpoint is not enough; it must also cross at 90°.
It must pass through the midpoint and cross at 90°.
It passes through the midpoint M, not through A; what is missing here is the 90°.

practice.question: An angle bisector cuts an angle into two angles of 35° each. How big was the whole angle?
practice.why: The two equal parts make the whole: 35° + 35° = 70°.
wrong: 35° is one part; the whole angle is two parts.
You halved 35°; add the two parts instead.
You doubled twice; there are only two parts of 35°.

entries.concept: congruent triangles, the SSS rule and CPCT
entries.evidence: Step 4 of the worked bisector says 'triangle PAQ ≅ triangle PBQ (SSS)' and the next lesson ends 'by CPCT', but congruence is not taught until class 7.

screens.title: Shapes that fit exactly
text: Put one 10 rupee coin on another. They match exactly: same shape, same size. Two shapes that fit exactly on top of each other are called congruent.
Two triangles are congruent when all three sides and all three angles of one match those of the other. In the lessons, an equals sign with a small wave on top means 'is congruent to'.
The order of the letters tells which corners match. 'Triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR' means A lies on P, B on Q and C on R. So AB matches PQ, BC matches QR and CA matches RP.
example: Triangle ABC has AB = 3 cm, BC = 4 cm, CA = 5 cm.
Triangle PQR is congruent to triangle ABC.
PQ matches AB, so PQ = 3 cm.
QR matches BC, so QR = 4 cm. RP matches CA, so RP = 5 cm.

check.question: Triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR. Which corner of PQR matches B?

screens.title: SSS and CPCT
text: Take three sticks of 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm. However you join them, you get the same triangle. So if the three sides of one triangle equal the three sides of another, the triangles are congruent. This rule is called SSS: side, side, side.
Once two triangles are congruent, every matching part is equal, the angles as well. The short name for this is CPCT: corresponding parts of congruent triangles. 'Corresponding' just means matching.
This is how compasses prove things. The arcs give equal sides, SSS gives congruent triangles, and CPCT gives equal angles. In the lessons a double arrow between two statements means 'so'.
example: To bisect an angle at O: an arc with centre O cuts the two arms at P and Q, so OP = OQ (same opening of the compasses).
Arcs with centres P and Q, drawn with one opening, cross at R, so PR = QR. Join OR: it is a side of both triangles OPR and OQR.
Three pairs of equal sides: triangles OPR and OQR are congruent by SSS.
So the matching angles POR and QOR are equal by CPCT. OR cuts the angle in half.

check.question: Two triangles each have sides of 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm. Are they congruent?

practice.question: Two shapes that fit exactly on top of each other are called
practice.why: Same shape and same size, fitting exactly: the shapes are congruent.
wrong: Corresponding means matching parts; the shapes themselves are congruent.
SSS is a rule that proves triangles congruent, not the name for the shapes.
CPCT says matching parts are equal; the shapes are called congruent.

practice.question: Triangle DEF is congruent to triangle XYZ. Which side matches EF?
practice.why: E matches Y and F matches Z (2nd and 3rd letters), so EF matches YZ.
wrong: XY matches DE, the first two letters.
ZX matches FD, the last and first letters.
DE is a side of the same triangle; look for the matching side in XYZ.

practice.question: Triangle ABC is congruent to triangle RPQ. Which corner matches C?
practice.why: The order of the letters tells the match: C is third, and the third letter of RPQ is Q.
wrong: R is first in RPQ, so it matches A; go by the order written, not the alphabet.
P is second in RPQ, so it matches B.
B is in the same triangle; the matching corner is in RPQ.

practice.question: Triangles ABC and PQR are congruent by SSS, with A on P, B on Q and C on R. Angle B = 50°. Which is true?
practice.why: B matches Q, and matching parts of congruent triangles are equal (CPCT), so angle Q = 50°.
wrong: P matches A, not B.
The angle is right, but SSS proves the triangles congruent; CPCT gives the equal angles.
R matches C, not B.

entries.concept: point, line segment and line, and naming them with letters
entries.evidence: The first lesson counts 'line segments' and 'lines' through points A, B, C and writes AB and BA, without saying what a point, a line segment or a line is.

screens.title: Points, line segments and lines
text: Make a dot on paper with a sharp pencil. The dot marks one place. It is called a point. We name a point with a capital letter, such as A.
Make another point B. Join A to B with a ruler. This straight path is a line segment. It has two ends, A and B. We call it AB. Going from B to A is the same path, so BA is the same segment.
A line is also straight, but it does not stop. It goes on and on both ways. We draw a small arrow at each end to show this. A line segment is a piece of a line.
example: Mark three points A, B and C, not in a row.
Join every pair: AB, AC, BC.

check.question: How many end points does a line segment have?

practice.question: A dot that marks one place is called
practice.why: A dot marks one place. It is called a point.
wrong: A line is a straight path that goes on and on, not one dot.
A line segment is a straight path with two ends, not one dot.
An arrow shows that a line goes on; the dot is a point.

practice.question: Which one goes on and on both ways?
practice.why: A line does not stop. It goes on and on both ways.
wrong: A point is just one place.
A line segment stops at its two ends.
A dot is a point, just one place.

practice.question: A line segment joins A and B. What can we say about AB and BA?
practice.why: Going from B to A is the same path as from A to B, so AB and BA are the same.
wrong: The path is the same both ways, so there is only one segment.
Both names are for the same path, so the length is the same.
It still has two ends, so it is a segment, not a line.

practice.question: A string is pulled tight between two nails. It is like
practice.why: The string is straight and has two ends, the nails. So it is like a line segment.
wrong: A point is one place; the string is a straight path.
A line never stops, but the string stops at the nails.
An arrow only shows that a line goes on; the string has two ends.

entries.concept: right angle (square corner)
entries.evidence: The lesson 'Parallel, perpendicular or neither' says perpendicular lines 'meet at a right angle', but right angles are first taught in class 4.

screens.title: The square corner
text: Look at the corner of your book page. It is a square corner. The corners of a door, a window and a floor tile are square corners too.
A square corner has a special name: a right angle. Two straight lines that meet and make a square corner are called perpendicular.

To test a corner, put the corner of a page into it. If both edges of the page lie along the two lines, it is a right angle. If the lines are closer together or wider apart than the page corner, it is not.
example: The top bar and the stem meet. A page corner fits exactly there.
So the bar and the stem are perpendicular.

check.question: Is the corner of a square tile a right angle?

practice.question: What is another name for a square corner?
practice.why: A square corner has a special name: a right angle.
wrong: The name is right angle; there is no left angle.
A straight line has no corner.
A square corner is made by two straight lines, so it is not round.

practice.question: Two straight lines meet and make a square corner. The lines are called
practice.why: Lines that make a square corner are called perpendicular.
wrong: Equal is about length; the word for a square corner is perpendicular.
They are straight, but the name for making a square corner is perpendicular.
Wide means more than a square corner; these lines are perpendicular.

practice.question: You put a page corner into a corner. The two lines are wider apart than the page corner. Is it a right angle?
options: No, it is wider than a square corner
Yes, all corners are right angles
Yes, wide corners are right angles
No, the lines are closer together
practice.why: A right angle fits the page corner exactly. This one is wider, so it is not a right angle.
wrong: Not all corners are right angles; only those that fit the page corner.
A right angle must fit the page corner exactly, not be wider.
It is not a right angle, but because the lines are wider apart, not closer.

practice.question: Which letter has a square corner?
practice.why: In L the two lines meet and a page corner fits exactly. That is a square corner.
wrong: In V the lines are closer together than a page corner.
O is round and has no corner.
In Z the lines at each corner are closer together than a page corner.

entries.concept: full turn, half turn and quarter turn
entries.evidence: The lesson on the four directions says 'a quarter turn right' and 'a half turn', but turns and quarters have not been taught by class 2.

screens.title: Full turn, half turn, quarter turn
text: Stand up and face the door. Now turn all the way round, once, until you face the door again. That is one full turn.
Face the door again. Turn until your back is to the door. That is a half turn. You now face the opposite way. Two half turns make one full turn.
A quarter turn is half of a half turn. Turn only until your shoulder points at the door. Four quarter turns make one full turn. A turn to the right goes the way your right hand points.
example: Ravi faces North. He makes a quarter turn right. Now he faces East.
He makes one more quarter turn right. Now he faces South.
Two quarter turns make a half turn, and South is the opposite of North.

check.question: How many quarter turns make one full turn?

practice.question: You turn all the way round and face the door again. What is this turn?
practice.why: Turning all the way round once is a full turn.
wrong: After a half turn your back is to the door.
After a quarter turn your shoulder points at the door.
You did turn, all the way round. That is a full turn.

practice.question: How many half turns make one full turn?
practice.why: Two half turns make one full turn.
wrong: 4 is for quarter turns. Two half turns make a full turn.
One half turn only gets you to face the opposite way.
Three is too many. Two half turns bring you back.

practice.question: Meena faces the door. She makes a half turn. What points at the door now?
practice.why: After a half turn you face the opposite way, so her back is to the door.
wrong: Her face points at the door after a full turn, not a half turn.
A shoulder points at the door after a quarter turn, not a half turn.
A shoulder points at the door after a quarter turn, not a half turn.

practice.question: Sita makes 2 quarter turns. This is the same as
practice.why: A quarter turn is half of a half turn, so 2 quarter turns make a half turn.
wrong: A full turn needs 4 quarter turns.
She made two quarter turns, not one.
Two full turns need 8 quarter turns.

entries.concept: names of polygons with 7 to 10 sides, and the base of a solid
entries.evidence: The first worked example asks for the edges of a 'nonagonal pyramid' and another for a 'heptagonal prism'; these names and the word 'base' are never explained.

screens.title: Naming shapes by their sides
text: A flat closed shape with straight sides is called a polygon. Its name tells how many sides it has: triangle 3, quadrilateral 4, pentagon 5, hexagon 6, heptagon 7, octagon 8, nonagon 9, decagon 10.
A polygon has as many corners as sides. A corner is also called a vertex. For more than one we say vertices.
A prism or a pyramid is named after its base. The base is the flat face it stands on. A hexagonal prism has a hexagon at the bottom and another at the top. A nonagonal pyramid stands on a nonagon.
example: Take a heptagonal pyramid. Its base is a heptagon, with 7 corners.
It has 1 more corner: the point at the top.

check.question: How many sides does an octagon have?

practice.question: What is a polygon with 7 sides called?
practice.why: The names go hexagon 6, heptagon 7, octagon 8. Seven sides is a heptagon.
wrong: A hexagon has 6 sides.
An octagon has 8 sides.
A nonagon has 9 sides.

practice.question: How many corners does a decagon have?
practice.why: A decagon has 10 sides, and a polygon has as many corners as sides.
wrong: 9 is for a nonagon; a decagon has 10.
8 is for an octagon; a decagon has 10.
A decagon has 10 sides, so 10 corners.

practice.question: How many vertices does an octagonal pyramid have in all?
practice.why: The base is an octagon with 8 corners, plus 1 point at the top: 8 + 1 = 9.
wrong: You forgot the point at the top.
You counted two octagons; a pyramid has one base and one top point.
An octagon has 8 corners, not 9; then add 1 for the top.

practice.question: A hexagonal prism stands on a table. What shape is the face it stands on?
practice.why: A prism is named after its base, so a hexagonal prism stands on a hexagon.
wrong: A heptagon has 7 sides; hexagonal means a hexagon, 6 sides.
A pentagon has 5 sides; hexagonal means a hexagon, 6 sides.
An octagon has 8 sides; hexagonal means a hexagon, 6 sides.

entries.concept: polyhedron, and what F, V and E stand for
entries.evidence: The lesson states 'For every polyhedron without holes, faces + vertices − edges = 2' without saying what a polyhedron is.

screens.title: What is a polyhedron?
text: Pick up a matchbox and a ball. The matchbox is made only of flat faces. The ball has no flat face at all.
A solid whose faces are all flat polygons is called a polyhedron. Cubes, cuboids, prisms and pyramids are polyhedra. A cylinder, a cone and a sphere are not, because they have curved surfaces.

A face is one flat surface. An edge is the line where two faces meet. A vertex is a corner where edges meet (for more than one we say vertices). In the formula, F is the number of faces, V the number of vertices and E the number of edges.
example: Count on a cube: F = 6 faces.

check.question: Is a cricket ball a polyhedron?

practice.question: In the formula, what does E stand for?
practice.why: E is the number of edges, the lines where two faces meet.
wrong: Faces are counted by F.
Vertices are counted by V.
The formula is about one solid; E counts its edges.

practice.question: Which of these is a polyhedron?
practice.why: A cuboid has only flat faces, so it is a polyhedron.
wrong: A cylinder has a curved surface, so it is not a polyhedron.
A cone has a curved surface, so it is not a polyhedron.
A sphere has no flat face at all.

practice.question: The line where two faces meet is called
practice.why: Two faces meet along a line, and that line is an edge.
wrong: A vertex is a corner point where edges meet.
A face is a flat surface, not a line.
A corner is a vertex, a point where edges meet.

practice.question: A solid has F = 5, V = 6 and E = 9. What is F + V − E?
wrong: You added all three; E is subtracted.
You worked out F + E − V; it is F + V − E.
You worked out V + E − F; it is F + V − E.

entries.concept: the square of a number and the square root (the signs ² and √)
entries.evidence: The first lesson writes 'c² = a² + b²' and '√5476 = 74' although squares and square roots are a class 8 skill and no lesson here says what ² or √ mean.

screens.title: Squaring a number
text: Lay tiles in a square: 3 rows with 3 tiles in each row. You need 3 × 3 = 9 tiles. A number multiplied by itself is called its square.
We write a small raised 2 for this. 3² is read '3 squared' and means 3 × 3 = 9. In the same way 5² = 5 × 5 = 25 and 10² = 10 × 10 = 100.
Be careful: 5² is not 5 × 2. It is 5 × 5. A square with side 5 cm has an area of 5² = 25 square centimetres, which is why it is called squaring.

check.question: What is 6²?

screens.title: Going back: the square root
text: A square garden has an area of 25 square metres. How long is one side? We need the number that, multiplied by itself, gives 25. That number is 5.
This backwards step is called taking the square root. Its sign is √. So √25 = 5, because 5 × 5 = 25. Also √49 = 7 and √100 = 10.
In a right-angled triangle we add the squares of the two shorter sides, and then take the square root to get the longest side.

check.question: What is √36?

practice.question: What does 8² mean?
practice.why: The small raised 2 means the number is multiplied by itself: 8 × 8.
wrong: The raised 2 does not mean times 2; it means 8 × 8.
Squaring multiplies the number by itself; it does not add it.
The raised 2 is not added; it means 8 × 8.

practice.question: What is 9²?
wrong: You did 9 × 2; squaring means 9 × 9.
You did 9 + 2; squaring means 9 × 9.
You did 9 × 8; multiply 9 by itself.

practice.question: What is √81?
wrong: You halved 81; find the number that multiplied by itself gives 81.
You doubled 81; the square root goes backwards from squaring.
You divided by 10; find the number that multiplied by itself gives 81.

practice.question: A right-angled triangle has shorter sides 6 cm and 8 cm. How long is the longest side?
wrong: You added the sides; add their squares, then take the square root.
You stopped at 100; take its square root.
You doubled the sides instead of squaring them; 6² is 36 and 8² is 64.

entries.concept: quadrilateral: its corners in order, opposite and neighbouring sides, and the parallel sign
entries.evidence: The first lesson classifies 'quadrilaterals' by 'opposite sides', names them ABCD and writes AB ∥ DC, but no earlier lesson says what a quadrilateral is or how its sides and angles are named.

screens.title: Four-sided shapes and their parts
text: A kite, a door and a tile all have 4 straight sides. Any flat closed shape with 4 straight sides is called a quadrilateral. It has 4 corners and 4 angles.

We name it by its corners in order, going round: ABCD. Its sides are AB, BC, CD and DA. Sides that share a corner are neighbouring sides, like AB and BC. Sides that do not touch are opposite sides, like AB and CD. Angles A and C are opposite angles.
Two sides are parallel when they run in the same direction and would never meet, like railway tracks. In the lessons, two small upright strokes between two names mean 'is parallel to'.
example: AB and DC are opposite sides. They are parallel and equal.
AD and BC are the other pair of opposite sides.
Angle A is opposite angle C.

check.question: In quadrilateral ABCD, which side is opposite to AB?

practice.question: Any flat closed shape with 4 straight sides is called
practice.why: Every flat closed shape with 4 straight sides is a quadrilateral.
wrong: A triangle has 3 sides.
A rectangle is only one kind; a kite also has 4 sides. The name for all of them is quadrilateral.
Parallel describes two sides that never meet, not a shape.

practice.question: In quadrilateral PQRS, which side is opposite to QR?
practice.why: The sides are PQ, QR, RS and SP. SP does not touch QR, so it is opposite.
wrong: PQ shares the corner Q with QR, so it is a neighbouring side.
RS shares the corner R with QR, so it is a neighbouring side.
QS joins two opposite corners; it is not a side.

practice.question: In quadrilateral ABCD, which pair are neighbouring sides?
practice.why: BC and CD share the corner C, so they are neighbouring sides.
wrong: AB and CD do not touch; they are opposite sides.
BC and DA do not touch; they are opposite sides.
AC and BD join opposite corners; they are not sides.

practice.question: Two railway tracks run in the same direction and never meet. They are
practice.why: Lines that run in the same direction and would never meet are parallel.
wrong: Neighbouring sides share a corner, so they do meet.
Equal is about length; never meeting is called parallel.
Closed describes a shape with no gap, not two lines.

entries.concept: a letter for an unknown length, and finding it from an equation
entries.evidence: The lesson on unknown sides writes 'AB = (2x + 4) cm, CD = (4x − 2) cm ... 2x + 4 = 4x − 2, so x = 3' with no steps; solving equations is a class 6 skill.

screens.title: A letter that hides a number
text: Sometimes we do not know a length yet. We give it a letter, such as x. The letter stands for a number.
2x means 2 × x. So 2x + 4 means: double the number, then add 4. If x is 3, then 2x + 4 = 2 × 3 + 4 = 10.
4x − 2 means: 4 times the number, then take away 2. If x is 3, then 4x − 2 = 12 − 2 = 10.

check.question: If x = 2, what is 3x?

screens.title: Finding the hidden number
text: Think of a balance. If both pans hold the same weight, it stays level. If you add the same thing to both pans, or take the same thing from both, it still stays level.
Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal. If they are 2x + 4 and 4x − 2, then 2x + 4 = 4x − 2. This is called an equation. We want the number x that makes both sides the same.
Do the same thing to both sides until x stands alone. Then put your x back into both sides to check.

check.question: If 3x = 12, what is x?

practice.question: What does 5x mean?
practice.why: A number written next to a letter means multiply: 5x = 5 × x.
wrong: Writing them together means times, not plus.
5 is not a tens digit here; 5x means 5 × x.
Nothing is taken away; 5x means 5 × x.

practice.question: If x = 4, what is 3x + 2?
wrong: You read 3x as 34; 3x means 3 × 4.
You added 2 to x first; multiply 3 × 4 first, then add 2.
You added 3 + 4 + 2; 3x means 3 × 4.

practice.question: If 2x + 3 = 11, what is x?
practice.why: Take 3 from both sides: 2x = 8. Divide both sides by 2: x = 4. Check: 2 × 4 + 3 = 11.
wrong: You found 2x = 8 but did not divide by 2.
You added 3 instead of taking 3 away, then halved.
You added 3 to 11; take 3 away from both sides, then divide by 2.

practice.question: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are 3x + 1 and x + 7. What is x?
practice.why: 3x + 1 = x + 7. Take x and 1 from both sides: 2x = 6, so x = 3. Check: 10 and 10.
wrong: You added x to get 4x = 8; take x away from both sides instead.
You found 2x = 6 but did not divide by 2.
You added 1 to 7; take 1 away from both sides to get 2x = 6.

entries.concept: names of flat shapes (triangle to hexagon)
entries.evidence: The first lesson asks about hexagons and pentagons, but no lesson before it says what these shape names mean (the skill that names triangle, square and circle comes later).

screens.title: Names of flat shapes
text: Look at a page of your book. Run your finger round its edge. The edge has straight parts. Each straight part is called a side.
A flat shape gets its name from how many sides it has. 3 sides: a triangle. 4 sides: a square or a rectangle. 5 sides: a pentagon. 6 sides: a hexagon.
A square has 4 sides that are all the same length. A rectangle has 2 long sides and 2 short sides. A circle is round, like a bangle. It has no straight sides at all.
example: A shape has straight sides. Count them: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

check.question: A shape has 6 straight sides. What is it called?

practice.question: A shape has 3 straight sides. What is it called?
practice.why: A shape with 3 sides is a triangle.
wrong: A square has 4 sides.
A pentagon has 5 sides.
A circle has no straight sides.

practice.question: How many sides does a pentagon have?
practice.why: A pentagon has 5 sides.
wrong: 4 sides make a square or a rectangle.
6 sides make a hexagon.
3 sides make a triangle.

practice.question: A shape has 4 sides: 2 long sides and 2 short sides. What is it?
practice.why: 4 sides with 2 long and 2 short make a rectangle.
wrong: A square has 4 sides that are all the same length.
A triangle has only 3 sides.
A hexagon has 6 sides.

practice.question: A roti is round. It has no straight sides. What shape is it?
practice.why: A round shape with no straight sides is a circle.
wrong: A square has 4 straight sides.
A triangle has 3 straight sides.
A rectangle has 4 straight sides.

entries.concept: names of solid shapes (cube, cuboid, pyramid, cylinder, cone, sphere)
entries.evidence: The lessons count faces of a cube, a cuboid, a square pyramid, a cylinder, a cone and a sphere before any lesson shows what these solids are.

screens.title: Names of solid shapes
text: A solid shape is a thing you can hold in your hand, like a ball or a box. It is not flat like a drawing.
A cube is like a dice: every face is a square of the same size. A cuboid is like a brick or a matchbox: a box shape. A sphere is like a ball: round all over.

A cylinder is like a tin or a pipe: a circle at each end. A cone is like an ice-cream cone: a circle at one end and a point at the other. A square pyramid has a square at the bottom and 4 triangles that meet at a point on top.
example: It is a box, but its faces are not all the same size.
So it is a cuboid, not a cube.

check.question: Is a ball a cube or a sphere?

practice.question: A dice is which solid shape?
practice.why: Every face of a dice is a square of the same size. So it is a cube.
wrong: A cuboid has faces that are not all the same size.
A cone has a point at one end.
A sphere is round all over, like a ball.

practice.question: Which solid has a circle at each end?
practice.why: A cylinder, like a tin, has a circle at each end.
wrong: A cone has a circle at one end only, and a point at the other.
A sphere is round all over. It has no ends.
A cube has square faces, not circles.

practice.question: A shoe box is a box. Its faces are not all the same size. What is it?
practice.why: A box whose faces are not all the same size is a cuboid.
wrong: A cube has faces that are all the same size.
A cylinder has a circle at each end.
A pyramid has triangles that meet at a point on top.

practice.question: A birthday cap has a circle at one end and a point at the other. What is it?
practice.why: A circle at one end and a point at the other make a cone.
wrong: A cylinder has a circle at both ends.
A square pyramid has a square at the bottom, not a circle.
A sphere is round all over and has no point.

entries.concept: regular polygon
entries.evidence: The lesson speaks of 'one regular pentagon (each corner 108°)' and 'a regular polygon' without saying what makes a polygon regular.

screens.title: Regular polygons
text: Look at a square floor tile. All 4 sides are the same length, and all 4 corners are the same angle. A polygon like this is called regular.

A regular polygon has all its sides equal and all its corner angles equal. A triangle with three equal sides is regular, and each of its corners is 60°. A square is regular, and each of its corners is 90°.
A rectangle that is longer than it is wide is not regular. Its corners are all 90°, but its sides are not all equal.
example: Put 4 square tiles round one point.
90° × 4 = 360°: a full turn, so there is no gap.

check.question: A triangle has sides of 3 cm, 3 cm and 5 cm. Is it regular?
check.answer: No, because its sides are not all equal.

practice.question: A polygon with all sides equal and all corner angles equal is called
practice.why: All sides equal and all corner angles equal: that is a regular polygon.
wrong: A long rectangle has equal corners but not equal sides.
Not every triangle has equal sides; the name for all such shapes is regular polygon.
A square is one regular polygon, but the name for all of them is regular polygon.

practice.question: One side of a regular triangle is 4 cm. How long is each of the other sides?
practice.why: A regular polygon has all its sides equal, so each side is 4 cm.
wrong: You doubled; all the sides are equal to 4 cm.
You halved; all the sides are equal to 4 cm.
60 is the corner angle in degrees, not the side length.

practice.question: A rectangle is 6 cm long and 2 cm wide. All its corners are 90°. Is it regular?
options: No, its corners are not equal
No, its sides are not all equal
practice.why: Regular needs equal corners and equal sides. Here the sides are 6 cm and 2 cm, so it is not regular.
wrong: Equal corners are not enough; the sides must all be equal too.
Having 4 sides does not make it regular; all sides must be equal.
Its corners are equal, all 90°; it is the sides that are not all equal.

practice.question: Each corner of a regular triangle is 60°. Six such corners are put round one point. How many degrees do they make?
practice.why: 60° × 6 = 360°. That is a full turn, so there is no gap.
wrong: You added 6 to 60; take 60° six times.
That is only three corners; there are six.
That is only five corners; there are six.

entries.concept: coordinates (x, y), the axes, the origin and a line such as x = 5
entries.evidence: The first worked example says 'P is at (0, 5) and the mirror line is x = 5'; x, y, the origin and the x-axis are used with no introduction (the coordinate plane is a class 8 skill).

screens.title: Two numbers find a point
text: In a cinema hall you find your seat with two things: which seat along the row, and which row. On a grid we find a point the same way, with two numbers.
Draw a number line lying flat. It is called the x-axis. Draw another standing up. It is called the y-axis. They cross where both show 0. That crossing point is called the origin, and its letter is O.

Every point gets two numbers in brackets, like (3, 2). The first number is x: how far across from O. The second number is y: how far up from O. The two numbers are called the coordinates of the point.
example: Start at O. Go 3 steps across to the right.
Then go 2 steps up. Mark the point.
(2, 3) is a different point: 2 across, then 3 up.

check.question: For the point (4, 1), how many steps up do you go?

screens.title: A line called x = 5
text: Mark the points (5, 0), (5, 1), (5, 2) and (5, 3). Each one is 5 steps across. They stand one above the other in a straight line going up and down.
That whole line is named x = 5, because every point on it has x equal to 5. In the same way, y = 5 is the line lying flat that is 5 steps up.
To see how far a point is from the line x = 5, compare its x with 5.
example: Is (5, 7) on the line x = 5? Its x is 5, so yes.
5 − 0 = 5, so it is 5 steps to the left of the line x = 5.

check.question: Is the point (5, 2) on the line x = 5?

practice.question: What is the point where the x-axis and the y-axis cross called?
practice.why: The axes cross where both show 0. That point is the origin, O.
wrong: The x-axis is the flat number line, not the crossing point.
The y-axis is the number line standing up, not the crossing point.
Coordinates are the two numbers of a point; the crossing point is the origin.

practice.question: How do you reach the point (2, 5) from O?
practice.why: The first number is across and the second is up: 2 across, then 5 up.
wrong: You swapped them; the first number is how far across.
Do not add the numbers; go 2 across and then 5 up.
You left out the first number; go 2 across first.

practice.question: Which point is on the line x = 4?
practice.why: Every point on the line x = 4 has x equal to 4. The first number of (4, 9) is 4.
wrong: Here y is 4; x is the first number, and it is 9.
Here y is 4; x is the first number, and it is 0.
The numbers add to 4, but x itself must be 4.

practice.question: How far is the point (1, 6) from the line x = 5?
practice.why: Compare its x with 5: 5 − 1 = 4, so it is 4 steps to the left of the line.
wrong: You compared y with 5; use x, the first number.
5 is the line itself; find the gap between x = 1 and 5.
You added 5 and 1; find the gap, 5 − 1.

entries.concept: negative numbers on a number line and on the grid
entries.evidence: The rotation lesson uses the point (−2, 3) and says 'change the sign of both coordinates', but negative numbers are first taught in class 5.
