text: Take small sets to see everything. Let A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {1, 4, 9, 10}, and f: A → B with f(x) = x².
The outputs are f(1) = 1, f(2) = 4, f(3) = 9. The set of outputs actually produced, {1, 4, 9}, is called the range. It sits inside the codomain B.

Different inputs gave different outputs here. Such a function is called one-one. But 10 is in the codomain and no input gives it. So f is not onto: 'onto' means every element of the codomain is used. A function that is both one-one and onto is called bijective.
Notice that the same formula can change its answer if you change the sets. With B = {1, 4, 9} this f would be onto. With A = {−1, 1} it would not be one-one, because f(−1) = f(1) = 1.
example: Outputs: 1, 4, 9. All different, so f is one-one.
10 is never an output, so f is not onto.

check.question: f(x) = x² with inputs −2 and 2. Do the two inputs give different outputs?
check.answer: No, both give 4 (so this f is not one-one)

practice.question: In f: A → B, what is the set A called?
practice.why: A is the set of inputs the function accepts. That is the domain.
wrong: The codomain is B, where the outputs may land. A is the domain.
The range is the set of outputs actually produced. A holds the inputs: the domain.
A holds the inputs, not the outputs. It is the domain.

practice.question: f(x) = 3x + 2. What is f(4)?
practice.why: Put 4 in place of x: 3 × 4 + 2 = 14.
wrong: You added 3 + 4 + 2. 3x means 3 × x: 3 × 4 + 2 = 14.
You added before multiplying. Multiply first: 3 × 4 = 12, then + 2 = 14.
You wrote 3 and 4 side by side as 34. 3x means 3 × 4 = 12, then + 2 = 14.

practice.question: A = {1, 2, 3}, B = {2, 4, 6, 8} and f: A → B with f(x) = 2x. What is the range of f?
practice.why: The range is the set of outputs actually produced: f(1) = 2, f(2) = 4, f(3) = 6.
wrong: That is the codomain B. No input gives 8, so 8 is not in the range.
That is the domain A. The range holds the outputs: 2, 4, 6.
8 is the output that is never used. The range is the outputs that are used: {2, 4, 6}.

practice.question: A = {1, 2}, B = {5, 6, 7} and f: A → B with f(x) = x + 4. Which is true?
options: f is onto but not one-one
f is one-one but not onto
f is neither one-one nor onto
practice.why: The outputs 5 and 6 are different, so f is one-one. 7 is never an output, so f is not onto.
wrong: It is the other way round: 5 and 6 are different outputs, and 7 is never used.
Bijective needs onto as well. No input gives 7, so f is not onto.
f(1) = 5 and f(2) = 6 are different, so f is one-one.

entries.concept: a relation as a set of ordered pairs, and an equivalence relation
entries.evidence: The lesson tests 'R = {(1, 1), (1, 3), (2, 2), (3, 1)}' and the next asks for 'the fewest pairs that make a relation an equivalence relation', but nothing in this topic says what the pairs of a relation mean or what an equivalence relation is.

screens.title: A relation is a list of who is related to whom
text: In a family, 'is a sister of' links some people to others. In maths, 'is less than' links some numbers to others. Such a link is called a relation.

To write a relation down exactly, list every linked pair. On the set A = {1, 2, 3}, the relation 'is less than' is R = {(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)}. The pair (1, 2) is in R because 1 is less than 2. The pair (2, 1) is not, because 2 is not less than 1. Order matters.
So a relation R on a set A is simply a set of ordered pairs of elements of A. (a, b) ∈ R is read 'a is related to b'. Any set of such pairs counts as a relation, even one with no rule in words.
Reflexive, symmetric and transitive are three questions about the list: is everything related to itself? Does every link go both ways? Do links chain together?
example: Reflexive? (1, 1) is not in R, so no.
Symmetric? (1, 2) is in R but (2, 1) is not, so no.
Transitive? (1, 2) and (2, 3) are in R, and so is (1, 3). Yes.

check.question: On A = {1, 2, 3}, is the pair (3, 1) in the relation 'is less than'?
check.answer: No, because 3 is not less than 1

screens.title: Equivalence: alike in some way
text: Some relations say 'these two are alike in some way': has the same birthday month as, has the same remainder as. A relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive all at once is called an equivalence relation.
An equivalence relation sorts the set into groups, called equivalence classes. Everything in a group is related to everything in that group (itself included), and nothing is related across groups.
That makes counting easy. In a group of n elements, each of the n is related to each of the n, so the group gives n × n = n² pairs.
example: A = {1, 2, 3}, relation 'both odd or both even'

check.question: An equivalence relation puts 3 elements all in one group. How many ordered pairs does it have?

practice.question: How is (a, b) ∈ R read?
practice.why: (a, b) ∈ R means the pair is in the list, read 'a is related to b'.
wrong: Order matters. (a, b) says a is related to b; the other way needs (b, a).
A pair in R does not say a and b are equal. It says a is related to b.
'Less than' was only one example of a relation. In general it reads 'a is related to b'.

practice.question: On A = {1, 2, 3}, which set is the relation 'is greater than'?
practice.why: List every pair whose first number is greater than the second: 2 > 1, 3 > 1, 3 > 2.
wrong: That is 'is less than'. Order matters: the greater number must come first.
No number is greater than itself. The pairs are (2, 1), (3, 1), (3, 2).
(3, 1) is missing: 3 is greater than 1 as well. List every linked pair.

practice.question: On A = {1, 2, 3}, R = {(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 2)}. Which is true?
practice.why: (1, 2) is in R but (2, 1) is not, so that link does not go both ways.
wrong: (1, 1), (2, 2) and (3, 3) are all in R, so it is reflexive. The gap is (2, 1).
Every chain here ends in a pair of R, such as (1, 1) and (1, 2) giving (1, 2). The gap is (2, 1).
That needs symmetric too. (1, 2) is in R but (2, 1) is not.

practice.question: Five students: 3 were born in May and 2 in June. The relation is 'has the same birthday month as'. How many ordered pairs does it have?
practice.why: A group of n gives n² pairs. 3² + 2² = 9 + 4 = 13.
wrong: 5² relates everyone to everyone. Nothing is related across the two groups: 9 + 4 = 13.
You added the group sizes. Each group of n gives n² pairs: 9 + 4 = 13.
You used n × 2. Each group gives n × n pairs: 3 × 3 + 2 × 2 = 13.

entries.concept: spread of data, deviation, and the symbols x̄, σ, σ², N
entries.evidence: The first worked example writes 'x̄ = Σfx/N' and 'σ² = Σfx²/N − x̄²' with no lesson saying why spread is measured or what x̄, σ and N stand for.

screens.title: Same mean, different spread
text: Two batters each play 3 matches. Asha scores 49, 50, 51. Bala scores 0, 50, 100. Both have a mean of 50. But Asha is steady and Bala is all over the place. The mean alone cannot show this.
We need a second number that tells how far the values are spread out from the mean. Such a number is called a measure of dispersion (dispersion means spread).
Start with the deviation of each value: value − mean. Asha's deviations are −1, 0, 1. Bala's are −50, 0, 50. Big deviations mean a big spread.
example: Bala's deviations are much bigger: his scores are more spread out.

check.question: All five values in a data set are 7. How far is each value from the mean?

screens.title: Variance σ² and standard deviation σ
text: Some symbols first. N is the number of values. x̄ is read 'x bar' and means the mean. σ is the small Greek letter sigma; it stands for the standard deviation, and σ² for the variance.

Deviations always add up to 0 (the minus ones cancel the plus ones), so we cannot just average them. Instead we square each deviation, which makes it positive, and then take the mean of the squares. That mean is the variance, σ².
Squaring changed the units (runs became 'square runs'), so we take the square root to come back. The square root of the variance is the standard deviation, σ.
A shortcut that gives the same variance: σ² = (the mean of the squares of the values) − x̄².

check.question: The variance of some data is 9. What is the standard deviation?

practice.question: What does σ stand for?
practice.why: σ is the small Greek letter sigma and stands for the standard deviation.
wrong: The variance is σ². σ alone is the standard deviation.
The mean is written x̄. σ is the standard deviation.
The number of values is N. σ is the standard deviation.

practice.question: The data are 3, 5, 7 and the mean is 5. What is the deviation of the value 3?
practice.why: Deviation = value − mean = 3 − 5 = −2.
wrong: You did mean − value. Deviation is value − mean: 3 − 5 = −2.
3 is the value itself. Subtract the mean: 3 − 5 = −2.
You added the mean. Deviation is value − mean: 3 − 5 = −2.

practice.question: The standard deviation of some data is 5. What is the variance?
practice.why: The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, so the variance is 5² = 25.
wrong: You took the root the wrong way. Variance = σ², so 5² = 25.
You doubled. The variance is the square of σ: 5 × 5 = 25.
You halved. The variance is the square of σ: 5 × 5 = 25.

practice.question: Shop A sells 48, 50 and 52 cups of tea on three days. Shop B sells 30, 50 and 70. Which is true?
options: Same mean, but B is more spread out
Same mean, but A is more spread out
practice.why: Both means are 50. B's deviations (−20, 0, 20) are bigger than A's (−2, 0, 2).
wrong: A's deviations are only −2, 0, 2. B's are −20, 0, 20, so B is more spread out.
30 + 50 + 70 = 150, and 150 ÷ 3 = 50, the same as A. Only the spread differs.
The mean alone cannot show spread. B's values lie much further from 50.

entries.concept: the symbol Σ, and what Σf and Σfx mean
entries.evidence: The lesson 'Mean of an ungrouped frequency distribution' says 'the total is Σfx and the number of observations is Σf' without ever saying what the symbol Σ means.

screens.title: Σ means 'add them all up'
text: In a frequency table, x is a value and f is its frequency: how many times that value occurs. If the score 3 has f = 2, then 3 was scored twice.
Σ is the Greek capital letter S, called sigma. S for Sum. It is an instruction: add up everything in that column. Σf means 'add all the frequencies'. That gives the number of values.

fx means f × x: the value, counted as many times as it occurs. Σfx means 'work out f × x in each row, then add them all'. That gives the total of all the values. So mean = Σfx ÷ Σf is simply total ÷ how many.

check.question: The frequencies in a table are 3, 4 and 5. What is Σf?

practice.question: What does Σ mean?
practice.why: Σ is sigma, S for Sum. It says: add up everything in that column.
wrong: Σ is S for Sum. It means add, not multiply.
The frequency is f. Σ is the instruction to add.
The mean is Σfx ÷ Σf. Σ by itself only means add them all up.

practice.question: The frequencies in a table are 2, 5 and 3. What is Σf?
practice.why: Σf means add all the frequencies: 2 + 5 + 3 = 10.
wrong: You multiplied. Σ means add: 2 + 5 + 3 = 10.
3 is how many rows there are. Add the frequencies: 2 + 5 + 3 = 10.
5 is only the biggest frequency. Add them all: 2 + 5 + 3 = 10.

practice.question: x: 1, 2 with f: 3, 2. What is Σfx?
practice.why: Work out f × x in each row, then add: 3 × 1 = 3, 2 × 2 = 4, and 3 + 4 = 7.
wrong: You added the columns first and then multiplied 5 × 3. Multiply in each row first: 3 + 4 = 7.
5 is Σf. For Σfx multiply f × x in each row: 3 + 4 = 7.
You added all four numbers. Multiply f × x in each row first: 3 + 4 = 7.

practice.question: In a test, 2 children scored 5 marks each and 3 children scored 10 marks each. What is the mean mark?
wrong: You averaged 5 and 10 and ignored the frequencies. Mean = Σfx ÷ Σf = 40 ÷ 5 = 8.
40 is the total, Σfx. Divide by Σf = 5 to get 8.
You divided by the 2 rows. Divide by Σf, the number of children: 40 ÷ 5 = 8.

entries.concept: cumulative frequency (a running total)
entries.evidence: The 'Median of grouped data' lesson says 'make a cumulative frequency column' and uses cf in the formula before cumulative frequency is explained (a later lesson in the same skill explains it).

screens.title: Cumulative frequency: counting as you go
text: A shopkeeper counts customers: 3 in the first hour, 5 in the second, 2 in the third. If you ask 'how many so far?', the answers are 3, then 3 + 5 = 8, then 8 + 2 = 10. This running total is the cumulative frequency, written cf.
In a table of marks with classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, the cumulative frequency of a class tells how many students scored less than the upper limit of that class.

It is how we find the middle. With n values, the middle is at position n/2. Go down the cf column: the first class whose cf reaches n/2 holds the median. It is called the median class. The last cf always equals n.
example: So 8 students scored less than 20, and n = 10.
n/2 = 5. The cf first reaches 5 in the class 10–20: that is the median class.

check.question: The frequencies are 4 and 6. What is the cumulative frequency of the second class?

practice.question: What is a cumulative frequency?
options: The upper limit of a class
A running total of the frequencies
practice.why: It answers 'how many so far?', so it is a running total.
wrong: It is not the biggest one. It is the total of all the frequencies so far.
The middle value is the median. The cf is a running total used to find it.
The upper limit is a mark, not a count. The cf counts how many lie below it.

practice.question: The frequencies of three classes are 2, 4 and 6. What is the cumulative frequency of the third class?
practice.why: Add as you go: 2, then 2 + 4 = 6, then 6 + 6 = 12.
wrong: 6 is the third class's own frequency. The cf adds all so far: 2 + 4 + 6 = 12.
You left out the first class. 2 + 4 + 6 = 12.
You multiplied. A running total adds: 2 + 4 + 6 = 12.

practice.question: Classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30 have f = 5, 7, 8. How many students scored less than 20?
practice.why: The cf of the class 10–20 is 5 + 7 = 12, and it counts everyone below 20.
wrong: 7 is only the class 10–20. 'Less than 20' also includes 0–10: 5 + 7 = 12.
20 is all the students, the last cf. Below 20 there are 5 + 7 = 12.
5 is the number below 10. Below 20 there are 5 + 7 = 12.

practice.question: Classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40 have f = 2, 3, 9, 6. Which is the median class?
practice.why: n = 20, so n/2 = 10. cf = 2, 5, 14, 20, and it first reaches 10 in the class 20–30.
wrong: n/2 = 10 is a position, not a mark. The cf there is only 5; it reaches 10 in 20–30.
Its cf is 20, but 20–30 reached 10 first, with cf 14. Take the first class that reaches n/2.
Its cf is only 2, far below n/2 = 10. The cf first reaches 10 in 20–30.

entries.concept: the bars | | (distance, ignoring sign)
entries.evidence: The worked example writes 'the distances |x − x̄| are ...' and the method says 'write each |x − x̄|' without saying what the upright bars mean.

screens.title: The bars | | mean 'how far'
text: Your house is 3 km east of school and your friend's is 3 km west. On a number line you are at 3 and your friend at −3. But both of you are the same distance from school: 3 km.
The bars | | ask only for that distance and drop the sign. |3| = 3 and |−3| = 3. This is called the absolute value. It is never negative.
So |x − x̄| means: how far the value x is from the mean x̄, no matter whether x is above or below it. The mean deviation is the mean of these distances.

check.question: What is |−7|?

practice.question: What is |−9|?
practice.why: The bars drop the sign and keep the distance from 0, which is 9.
wrong: An absolute value is never negative. The bars drop the sign: 9.
The bars do not cancel the number. −9 is 9 away from 0.
Do not square to remove the sign. Just drop the sign: 9.

practice.question: x = 3 and x̄ = 8. What is |x − x̄|?
practice.why: 3 − 8 = −5, and the bars drop the sign: 5.
wrong: That is x − x̄ before the bars. A distance is never negative: 5.
You added. Subtract first, 3 − 8 = −5, then drop the sign: 5.
You multiplied. |x − x̄| is how far 3 is from 8: 5.

practice.question: The data are 1, 5, 9 and the mean is 5. What is the mean deviation?
practice.why: The distances |x − x̄| are 4, 0, 4. They add up to 8, and 8 ÷ 3 = 8/3.
wrong: You kept the signs, so −4 and 4 cancelled. Use the distances 4, 0, 4: 8 ÷ 3.
8 is the total of the distances. Divide by the 3 values: 8/3.
You divided by 2 and left out the value with distance 0. There are 3 values: 8 ÷ 3.

practice.question: Town A is 8 km east of a temple, at 8 on a number line. Town B is 5 km west, at −5. How far is B from the temple?
practice.why: Distance drops the sign: |−5| = 5.
wrong: A distance is never negative. |−5| = 5.
13 km is from A to B. From the temple to B it is |−5| = 5.
You did 8 − 5. B's distance from the temple is just |−5| = 5.

entries.concept: what an average (the mean) is
entries.evidence: The lessons 'The mean of data in a frequency table' and 'The median is not the mean ... they are different averages' use the mean and the word average before the mean is introduced (MATH.statistics.averages-intro comes after it).

screens.title: One number for a whole group: the mean
text: Three friends have 2, 4 and 6 sweets. About how many sweets is that for each friend? Put all the sweets in one pile: 2 + 4 + 6 = 12. Now share the pile equally among the 3 friends: each gets 4.
That equal share, 4, is called the mean. Mean = the total of all the values ÷ how many values there are.

An average is one number that stands for a whole set of numbers. The mean is one kind of average. The median (the middle value) and the mode (the most common value) are two other kinds. They can give different answers for the same data.

check.question: What is the mean of 5 and 7?

practice.question: How do you find the mean?
options: Total of all the values ÷ how many values there are
practice.why: The mean is the equal share: put everything in one pile and share it equally.
wrong: The middle value is the median. The mean is total ÷ how many.
The most common value is the mode. The mean is total ÷ how many.
One value cannot stand for all. The mean is total ÷ how many.

practice.question: What is the mean of 3, 5 and 10?
practice.why: Total: 3 + 5 + 10 = 18. There are 3 values, so 18 ÷ 3 = 6.
wrong: 18 is the total. Divide it by the 3 values: 6.
5 is the middle value, the median. Mean = 18 ÷ 3 = 6.
You divided by 2. There are 3 values: 18 ÷ 3 = 6.

practice.question: In three games Arun scores 0, 3 and 9 goals. What is his mean score?
practice.why: Total: 0 + 3 + 9 = 12. The 0 is still a value, so divide by 3: 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
wrong: You left out the game with 0 and divided by 2. There are 3 games: 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
12 is the total. Share it over the 3 games: 4.
3 is the middle value, the median. Mean = 12 ÷ 3 = 4.

practice.question: Meena reads 10, 20, 30 and 40 pages on four days. What is the mean number of pages a day?
practice.why: Total: 10 + 20 + 30 + 40 = 100. There are 4 days, so 100 ÷ 4 = 25.
wrong: 100 is the total. Divide it by the 4 days: 25.
You divided by 2. There are 4 days: 100 ÷ 4 = 25.
You divided by 5. Count the values: there are 4, so 100 ÷ 4 = 25.

entries.concept: quartiles and the interquartile range
entries.evidence: The lesson asks to 'estimate the upper quartile (Q3)' and says 'the lower quartile is at n/4' and 'the interquartile range is Q3 − Q1', but never says what a quartile is or what the range tells us.

screens.title: Quartiles cut the data into four equal parts
text: Line up 40 students from the lowest mark to the highest. The median is the mark at the middle of the line: half the students are below it.

Now cut each half in half again. The mark a quarter of the way along the line is the lower quartile, Q1: one quarter of the students are below it. The mark three quarters of the way along is the upper quartile, Q3: three quarters are below it. Quarter, quartile: the same idea.
So with n students, Q1 is at position n/4, the median at n/2 and Q3 at 3n/4. On an ogive you find that position on the upright axis, go across to the curve and read the mark below.
The interquartile range is Q3 − Q1. It is the spread of the middle half of the students. A small value means the middle students have nearly the same marks.
example: Q1 is at position 40 ÷ 4 = 10, the median at 20, Q3 at 30.
Suppose the ogive gives Q1 = 45 marks and Q3 = 65 marks.

check.question: There are 80 students. At which position is the lower quartile Q1?

practice.question: What is the interquartile range?
practice.why: It is the upper quartile minus the lower quartile: the spread of the middle half.
wrong: A range is a difference, not a sum. It is Q3 − Q1.
That covers only one quarter of the students. The middle half is Q3 − Q1.
That is the spread of all the students. The interquartile range uses only Q3 − Q1.

practice.question: There are 60 students. At which position is the lower quartile Q1?
practice.why: Q1 is at position n/4 = 60 ÷ 4 = 15.
wrong: 30 is n/2, the position of the median. Q1 is at n/4 = 15.
45 is 3n/4, the position of Q3. Q1 is at n/4 = 15.
You divided by 3. Quartiles cut into four parts: 60 ÷ 4 = 15.

practice.question: There are 20 students. At which position is the upper quartile Q3?
practice.why: Q3 is at position 3n/4 = 3 × 20 ÷ 4 = 15.
wrong: 5 is n/4, the position of Q1. Q3 is three quarters along: 15.
10 is n/2, the position of the median. Q3 is at 3n/4 = 15.
You forgot to divide by 4. 3 × 20 ÷ 4 = 15.

practice.question: For the heights of 100 plants, an ogive gives Q1 = 12 cm and Q3 = 20 cm. What is the interquartile range?
practice.why: Interquartile range = Q3 − Q1 = 20 − 12 = 8 cm.
wrong: You added. The range is the difference Q3 − Q1 = 8 cm.
16 is halfway between the quartiles. The range is Q3 − Q1 = 8 cm.
Do not halve the difference. Q3 − Q1 = 20 − 12 = 8 cm.

entries.concept: degrees, and a full turn of 360°
entries.evidence: The sector-angle lesson says 'the whole circle, 360°' and computes 11/20 of 360° in class 4, before measuring angles in degrees is taught (class 5, MATH.geometry.angle-measure).

screens.title: A full turn is 360°
text: Stand up and turn all the way round until you face the same way again. That is one full turn. People long ago cut a full turn into 360 tiny equal turns. Each tiny turn is called one degree, written 1°.
So a full turn is 360°. Half a turn is 180°. A quarter turn, the corner of a book, is 90°.

A slice of a pie chart is called a sector. Its pointed corner sits at the centre of the circle. The size of that corner, in degrees, is the sector's angle. All the slices together go once round the centre, so their angles add up to 360°.
example: A quarter of a class likes mangoes.
Their slice is a quarter of the circle.
The mango sector has an angle of 90°.

check.question: Half the class comes by bus. What is the angle of the bus sector?

practice.question: How many degrees are there in one full turn?
practice.why: A full turn is cut into 360 tiny equal turns, so it is 360°.
wrong: 180° is half a turn. A full turn is 360°.
90° is a quarter turn. A full turn is 360°.
A full turn is not cut into 100 parts. It is cut into 360: 360°.

practice.question: You make a quarter turn. Then you make one more quarter turn. How many degrees have you turned?
practice.why: A quarter turn is 90°. 90° + 90° = 180°, which is half a turn.
wrong: That is only one quarter turn. Two of them make 90° + 90° = 180°.
360° is a full turn, which is four quarter turns. Two make 180°.
You halved 90°. Two quarter turns add: 90° + 90° = 180°.

practice.question: A pie chart has three sectors. Two of them are 100° and 60°. What is the angle of the third sector?
wrong: 160° is the two sectors together. Take it from 360°: 200°.
You took 160° from 180°. The slices go all the way round: 360° − 160° = 200°.
You did 100° − 60°. Add the two, then take from 360°: 200°.

practice.question: Three quarters of a class like cricket. What is the angle of the cricket sector?
practice.why: One quarter of 360° is 90°. Three quarters is 90° + 90° + 90° = 270°.
wrong: 90° is one quarter. Three quarters is 3 × 90° = 270°.
180° is half the circle. Three quarters is 3 × 90° = 270°.
The circle has 360 degrees, not 100. Three quarters of 360° is 270°.

entries.concept: line of sight, angle of elevation and angle of depression
entries.evidence: The first lesson says 'the angle of elevation (or depression, which is equal to it by alternate angles) links two of its sides' without saying what either angle is.

screens.title: Looking up and looking down
text: Stand on level ground and look straight ahead. Your eyes look along a level line, called the horizontal. Now look up at the top of a tree. The straight line from your eye to the treetop is the line of sight.
The angle of elevation is the angle through which you raise your eyes: the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight, when the object is above you.
Now stand on a balcony and look down at a ball on the ground. The angle through which you lower your eyes from the horizontal is the angle of depression.

In both cases the height, the distance along the ground and the line of sight make a right triangle. The line of sight is its hypotenuse. (We usually ignore the height of the person's eyes unless it is given.)
example: You stand 10 m from a tree. The angle of elevation of its top is 45°.
Opposite = the tree's height h. Adjacent = 10 m.

check.question: From a bridge you look down at a boat. Is the angle between the horizontal and your line of sight an angle of elevation or of depression?

practice.question: What is the straight line from your eye to the object you are looking at called?
practice.why: The line from the eye to the object is the line of sight.
wrong: The horizontal is the level line straight ahead. The line to the object is the line of sight.
That is an angle, not a line. The line itself is the line of sight.
The height is the upright side. The line from eye to object is the line of sight.

practice.question: You stand on the ground and look up at a kite. What is the angle between the horizontal and your line of sight called?
practice.why: The kite is above you, so you raise your eyes: an angle of elevation.
wrong: Depression is for looking down. You look up at the kite: elevation.
The right angle is where the height meets the ground. Raising your eyes gives the angle of elevation.
The hypotenuse is the line of sight, a side. The angle is the angle of elevation.

practice.question: Ravi looks down from a window at a dog on the ground. The dog looks up at Ravi. Which is right?
options: Ravi: angle of elevation. Dog: angle of depression.
Ravi: angle of depression. Dog: angle of elevation.
practice.why: Ravi lowers his eyes (depression). The dog raises its eyes (elevation).
wrong: These are swapped. Looking down is depression; looking up is elevation.
Ravi looks down, so his is an angle of depression.
The dog looks up, so its angle is an angle of elevation.

practice.question: A boy stands 15 m from a flagpole. The angle of elevation of its top is 45°. How tall is the flagpole? (tan 45° = 1)
practice.why: tan 45° = height ÷ 15 and tan 45° = 1, so the height is 15 m.
wrong: 45 is the angle, not a length. height = 15 × tan 45° = 15 m.
Do not double. height ÷ 15 = 1, so the height is 15 m.
Do not halve. tan 45° = 1, so the height equals the distance: 15 m.

entries.concept: what an identity is, and where sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 comes from
entries.evidence: The skill starts by factorising sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 and says 'sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 ... does almost everything', but no lesson says what an identity is or why these are true.

screens.title: An identity is true for every angle
text: An equation like sin θ = 1/2 is true only for some angles. An identity is an equation that is true for every angle you put in. The most important one comes straight from Pythagoras.
In a right triangle, opposite² + adjacent² = hypotenuse². Divide every term by hypotenuse². You get (opposite ÷ hypotenuse)² + (adjacent ÷ hypotenuse)² = 1.
But opposite ÷ hypotenuse is sin θ and adjacent ÷ hypotenuse is cos θ. So sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, whatever the angle θ is.
example: Triangle 3, 4, 5 with θ facing the side 3: sin θ = 3/5, cos θ = 4/5

check.question: For some angle, sin²θ = 0.36. What is cos²θ?

screens.title: Two more identities from the same triangle
text: Start again from opposite² + adjacent² = hypotenuse², but this time divide every term by adjacent². You get (opposite ÷ adjacent)² + 1 = (hypotenuse ÷ adjacent)².
opposite ÷ adjacent is tan θ, and hypotenuse ÷ adjacent is sec θ. So tan²θ + 1 = sec²θ, which is the same as sec²θ − tan²θ = 1.
Dividing by opposite² instead gives 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ, the same as cosec²θ − cot²θ = 1. All three identities are Pythagoras' theorem in different clothes.
example: Triangle 3, 4, 5 with θ facing the side 3: tan θ = 3/4, sec θ = 5/4

check.question: If tan²θ = 3, what is sec²θ?

practice.question: An identity is an equation that is true for
options: only the angles of a 3, 4, 5 triangle
practice.why: An identity is true for every angle you put in.
wrong: That is an ordinary equation, like sin θ = 1/2. An identity holds for every angle.
The triangle was just one check. An identity holds for every angle.
An identity is always true, not never true.

practice.question: For some angle, sin²θ = 0.25. What is cos²θ?
practice.why: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, so cos²θ = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75.
wrong: They are not equal; they add up to 1. 1 − 0.25 = 0.75.
You added. cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ = 0.75.
0.5 is sin θ, the root of 0.25. cos²θ = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75.

practice.question: If sec²θ = 10, what is tan²θ?
practice.why: sec²θ − tan²θ = 1, so tan²θ = 10 − 1 = 9.
wrong: You added 1. tan²θ + 1 = sec²θ, so tan²θ = 10 − 1 = 9.
3 is tan θ. The question asks for tan²θ, which is 9.
sec and tan are not linked by turning upside down. Use sec²θ − tan²θ = 1.

practice.question: A right triangle has sides 5, 12 and 13. The angle θ faces the side 5. What is sin²θ + cos²θ?
wrong: You added sin θ and cos θ without squaring. Square first: 25/169 + 144/169 = 1.
You added 25 + 144 but left out the 169 underneath. 169/169 = 1.
You subtracted the squares. The identity adds them: 169/169 = 1.

entries.concept: what sin⁻¹ x means, and reading [ , ] and ( , )
entries.evidence: The first lesson asks for 'the domain of sin⁻¹' and lists ranges such as [−π/2, π/2] without saying that sin⁻¹ x is 'the angle whose sine is x' or how the brackets are read.

screens.title: Going backwards: from the ratio to the angle
text: So far you went forwards: give an angle, get a ratio. sin 30° = 1/2. The inverse goes backwards: give the ratio, get the angle. 'Which angle has sine 1/2?' The answer is 30°, or π/6 radians.
This backwards question is written sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6. Read sin⁻¹ x as 'the angle whose sine is x'. In the same way, cos⁻¹ x is the angle whose cosine is x and tan⁻¹ x is the angle whose tangent is x.
Careful: the small −1 here does not mean 'one divided by'. 1 ÷ sin x is cosec x, a different thing.

There is a difficulty. Many angles have the same sine: sin 30° = 1/2 and sin 150° = 1/2. A function must give one answer, so everyone agrees to pick the angle from one fixed stretch of angles. The angle picked is called the principal value.

check.question: sin 90° = 1. What is sin⁻¹(1)?

screens.title: Which numbers go in, which angles come out
text: The domain of a function is the set of numbers you are allowed to put in. The range is the set of answers that come out.
A sine is never more than 1 or less than −1. So 'the angle whose sine is 2' does not exist: you may only put numbers from −1 to 1 into sin⁻¹.

Such a stretch of numbers is written with brackets. [−1, 1] means all numbers from −1 to 1, with both ends included. A round bracket leaves the end out: (0, π) means all numbers between 0 and π, but not 0 or π themselves.
So 'sin⁻¹ has domain [−1, 1] and range [−π/2, π/2]' means: put in any number from −1 to 1, and the answer is an angle from −π/2 to π/2 (from −90° to 90°).
example: sin⁻¹(1/2): 1/2 lies in [−1, 1], so it is allowed. The answer π/6 lies in [−π/2, π/2].
sin⁻¹(2): 2 is outside [−1, 1], so it is not defined.

check.question: Is the number 1 inside the interval (0, 1)?
check.answer: No. The round bracket leaves 1 out.

practice.question: How is sin⁻¹ x read?
options: The angle whose sine is x
The sine of the angle x
practice.why: The inverse goes backwards: give the ratio x, get the angle.
wrong: The small −1 does not mean 'one divided by'. 1 ÷ sin x is cosec x.
That is sin x, going forwards. sin⁻¹ goes backwards, from ratio to angle.
The −1 is not a subtraction. sin⁻¹ x is the angle whose sine is x.

practice.question: tan 60° = √3. What is tan⁻¹(√3)?
practice.why: tan⁻¹(√3) is the angle whose tangent is √3. That angle is 60° = π/3.
wrong: The −1 does not mean 'one divided by'. tan⁻¹ gives an angle: 60°.
45° is tan⁻¹(1). The angle whose tangent is √3 is 60°.
tan 30° is 1/√3, not √3. The angle whose tangent is √3 is 60°.

practice.question: sin 60° = √3/2 and sin 120° = √3/2. What is the principal value sin⁻¹(√3/2)?
practice.why: The answer must lie in [−π/2, π/2], that is from −90° to 90°. Only 60° does.
wrong: 120° is outside −90° to 90°. The principal value is 60°.
A function gives one answer. The one inside [−π/2, π/2] is 60°.
That is 1 ÷ (√3/2). sin⁻¹ asks for an angle, 60°.

practice.question: Which number lies in the interval [2, 7)?
practice.why: The square bracket includes the end 2.
wrong: The round bracket leaves the end 7 out.
1.9 is less than 2, so it is outside the interval.
7.5 is more than 7, so it is outside the interval.

entries.concept: sin and cos of angles beyond 90° (the unit circle and the four quadrants)
entries.evidence: This skill uses sin(π − θ) = sin θ, negative angles and values like cos⁻¹ in [0, π], and the next skills use 'reference angle and quadrant sign', but sin and cos were only defined for acute angles of a right triangle; the unit-circle definition appears only in a late lesson of MATH.trigonometry.functions, the last skill in the order.

screens.title: Sine and cosine for any angle
text: In a right triangle the angle θ is always between 0° and 90°. So what could sin 150° or cos 180° mean? We need a bigger definition that agrees with the old one.

Draw a circle of radius 1 with its centre at the origin of the x and y axes. This is the unit circle. Start at the point (1, 0) and turn through the angle θ, anticlockwise. You arrive at a point P on the circle.
Definition: cos θ is the x-coordinate of P and sin θ is the y-coordinate of P. And tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ.

For an acute angle this is the old definition: drop a line from P to the x-axis and you get a right triangle with hypotenuse 1, adjacent side x and opposite side y. So cos θ = x ÷ 1 and sin θ = y ÷ 1. But the new definition works for every angle, even negative ones.
example: θ = 90°: P is at the top of the circle, (0, 1). So cos 90° = 0 and sin 90° = 1.

check.question: After a full turn, θ = 360°, the point P is back at (1, 0). What is sin 360°?

screens.title: Four quadrants decide the sign
text: The two axes cut the plane into four quarters, called quadrants. They are numbered I, II, III, IV going anticlockwise, starting at the top right. Angles from 0° to 90° land in quadrant I, 90° to 180° in II, 180° to 270° in III and 270° to 360° in IV.

The signs come from the coordinates of P. In quadrant I, x and y are both positive, so sin and cos are both positive. In II, x is negative and y positive: cos is negative, sin positive. In III both are negative (so tan, their quotient, is positive). In IV, x is positive and y negative: cos positive, sin negative.

The size comes from the reference angle: the acute angle between the line OP and the x-axis (O is the origin, the centre of the circle). P sits at the same height and the same distance sideways as the point for the reference angle, only perhaps on the other side.
example: θ = 150° is in quadrant II. Its reference angle is 180° − 150° = 30°.
For 30°, the point is (√3/2, 1/2). For 150° it is the mirror image: (−√3/2, 1/2).
This also shows sin(180° − θ) = sin θ.

check.question: The angle 100° is in quadrant II. Is cos 100° positive or negative?

practice.question: On the unit circle, turning through θ brings you to the point P. What is cos θ?
options: y ÷ x for the point P
practice.why: By definition cos θ is the x-coordinate of P.
wrong: The y-coordinate is sin θ. cos θ is the x-coordinate.
The radius is always 1. cos θ is the x-coordinate of P.
y ÷ x is sin θ ÷ cos θ, which is tan θ. cos θ is just x.

practice.question: For some angle θ the point P on the unit circle is (0.6, 0.8). What is sin θ?
practice.why: sin θ is the y-coordinate of P, which is 0.8.
wrong: 0.6 is the x-coordinate, which is cos θ. sin θ is the y-coordinate: 0.8.
1 is the radius. sin θ is the y-coordinate: 0.8.
0.6 ÷ 0.8 is x ÷ y. sin θ is simply the y-coordinate: 0.8.

practice.question: The angle 200° is in quadrant III. Which is true?
options: sin 200° and cos 200° are both positive
sin 200° is positive and cos 200° is negative
sin 200° is negative and cos 200° is positive
sin 200° and cos 200° are both negative
practice.why: In quadrant III both x and y are negative, so cos and sin are both negative.
wrong: That is quadrant I. In quadrant III both coordinates are negative.
That is quadrant II. In quadrant III y is negative too.
That is quadrant IV. In quadrant III x is negative too.

practice.question: For 30° the point on the unit circle is (√3/2, 1/2). What is cos 330°?
practice.why: 330° is in quadrant IV with reference angle 360° − 330° = 30°. There x is positive, so cos 330° = √3/2.
wrong: In quadrant IV x is positive. Only sin is negative there.
1/2 is the height, the y-part. cos is the x-coordinate: √3/2.
−1/2 is sin 330°, the y-coordinate. cos is the x-coordinate: √3/2.

entries.concept: an angle as an amount of turning (negative angles, more than 360°)
entries.evidence: The first worked example converts −720° and a later one −695°, but until now angles were corners of triangles between 0° and 180°; no lesson says what a negative angle or an angle beyond a full turn is.

screens.title: Angles that measure turning
text: Think of the hand of a clock, or a wheel. An angle can measure how much something has turned, not just the size of a corner.

Start with a ray pointing to the right. Turn it about its end point. Turning anticlockwise (the opposite way to a clock's hands) is counted as positive. Turning clockwise is counted as negative. So −90° is a quarter turn clockwise.
A turning thing can keep going. One full turn is 360°, two full turns are 720°, and 450° is one full turn and then 90° more. The ray for 450° ends in the same place as the ray for 90°.
So angles can be any number: big, small or negative.
example: 450° = 360° + 90°: one full turn, then a quarter turn.
−90° and 270° end in the same place, pointing straight down.

check.question: A wheel turns −360°. Where does a mark on it end up?
check.answer: Exactly where it started (one full turn clockwise)

practice.question: How is turning anticlockwise counted?
practice.why: Anticlockwise turning is positive. Clockwise turning is negative.
wrong: Negative is for clockwise turning. Anticlockwise is positive.
Zero means no turning at all. Anticlockwise turning is positive.
The direction gives the sign, not the size. Anticlockwise is positive.

practice.question: A ray makes half a turn clockwise. What is the angle?
practice.why: Half a turn is 180°, and clockwise is negative: −180°.
wrong: The size is right, but clockwise turning is negative: −180°.
−90° is a quarter turn clockwise. Half a turn is −180°.
−360° is a full turn clockwise. Half a turn is −180°.

practice.question: The ray for 400° ends in the same place as the ray for
practice.why: 400° = 360° + 40°: one full turn and then 40° more.
wrong: After the full turn the extra 40° is still anticlockwise, so it is 40°, not −40°.
You took away 180°. A half turn changes the place; take away a full turn: 400° − 360° = 40°.
140° is 180° − 40°. Just take away one full turn: 400° − 360° = 40°.

practice.question: The minute hand of a clock moves for 15 minutes. Through what angle does it turn, as a signed angle (clockwise is negative)?
practice.why: 15 minutes is a quarter of the way round, and a clock hand turns clockwise: −90°.
wrong: The size is right, but a clock hand turns clockwise, which is negative: −90°.
15 minutes is not 15 degrees. It is a quarter turn: −90°.
−180° is half a turn, which takes 30 minutes. 15 minutes is −90°.

entries.concept: what a radian is
entries.evidence: The lesson gives only 'one radian is the angle whose arc equals the radius' before using π radians = 180°; nothing shows what that looks like or why π appears.

screens.title: Measuring an angle with the radius
text: Degrees cut a full turn into 360 parts, a number people chose long ago. There is a more natural way that uses the circle itself.

Draw a circle. Take a piece of string as long as the radius and lay it along the edge of the circle. The curved piece of the edge it covers is an arc. Join the two ends of the arc to the centre. The angle at the centre is 1 radian. It is a little less than 60°.
So the angle in radians tells how many radius-lengths fit along the arc: angle = arc length ÷ radius.
All the way round, the arc is the whole circumference, 2π × radius. That is 2π radius-lengths. So a full turn is 2π radians, which means 2π radians = 360° and π radians = 180°.
example: Radius 5 cm, arc 5 cm: angle = 5 ÷ 5 = 1 radian
Radius 5 cm, arc 10 cm: angle = 10 ÷ 5 = 2 radians
Half the circle: arc = π × 5 cm, so angle = π radians = 180°

check.question: An arc is 3 times as long as the radius. What is the angle at the centre, in radians?

practice.question: π radians is the same as
practice.why: A full turn is 2π radians = 360°, so π radians = 180°.
wrong: 360° is 2π radians. π radians is half of that: 180°.
90° is π/2 radians. π radians is 180°.
π is about 3.14 radians, not degrees. π radians = 180°.

practice.question: A circle has radius 4 cm. An arc of it is 12 cm long. What is the angle at the centre?
practice.why: angle = arc length ÷ radius = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 radians.
wrong: You multiplied. angle = arc ÷ radius = 12 ÷ 4 = 3.
You divided the wrong way round. It is arc ÷ radius = 12 ÷ 4 = 3.
You subtracted. angle = arc ÷ radius = 12 ÷ 4 = 3.

practice.question: How many radians are there in one full turn?
practice.why: The whole circumference is 2π × radius, which is 2π radius-lengths.
wrong: π radians is only half a turn, 180°. A full turn is 2π.
360 is the number of degrees. In radians a full turn is 2π.
The π is missing. The circumference is 2π radius-lengths, so it is 2π.

practice.question: A goat is tied to a post with a rope 10 m long. With the rope tight, it walks 5 m along its circle. Through what angle does the rope turn?
practice.why: angle = arc length ÷ radius = 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5 radian.
wrong: You did radius ÷ arc. It is arc ÷ radius = 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5.
You multiplied. angle = arc ÷ radius = 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5.
5 m is the arc length. Divide it by the radius 10 m: 0.5.

entries.concept: what sin, cos and tan are (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse)
entries.evidence: The first lesson starts with 'the ratios of 30°, 45° and 60°' and evaluates sin 45° sin 30°; no lesson says what sin, cos and tan are or names the sides of a right triangle.

screens.title: Naming the sides of a right triangle
text: Lean a ladder against a wall. The ladder, the wall and the ground make a triangle with a right angle (90°) where the wall meets the ground.
Look at the angle the ladder makes with the ground. Call it θ (a Greek letter, said 'theeta'; it is just a name for an angle).

From the angle θ, each side gets a name. The hypotenuse is the longest side, the one facing the right angle: the ladder. The opposite side is the one across from θ, not touching it: the wall. The adjacent side is the one next to θ that is not the hypotenuse: the ground.
If you look from the other sharp angle (at the top of the ladder), opposite and adjacent swap. The hypotenuse stays the same.
example: A right triangle has sides 3, 4 and 5. The angle θ faces the side 3.

check.question: In a right triangle with sides 5, 12 and 13, which side is the hypotenuse?

screens.title: sin, cos and tan are three divisions
text: Make the ladder triangle bigger or smaller but keep the angle θ the same. Every side grows or shrinks by the same factor (the triangles are similar). So opposite ÷ hypotenuse does not change. That number depends only on the angle θ.

We give three such divisions names. sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse. cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse. tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent. They are read 'sine', 'cosine' and 'tangent' of θ, and are called trigonometric ratios.
Why bother? If you know an angle and one side, these ratios give the other sides. That is how people find the height of a tower or a hill without climbing it.
sin 30° = 1/2 means: in every right triangle with a 30° angle, the side opposite that angle is half the hypotenuse.
example: Sides 3, 4, 5 with θ facing the side 3.

check.question: In a right triangle, the side opposite θ is 5 and the hypotenuse is 13. What is sin θ?

practice.question: In a right triangle, what is the side facing the right angle called?
practice.why: The hypotenuse is the longest side, the one facing the right angle.
wrong: The opposite side faces the angle θ. The side facing the right angle is the hypotenuse.
The adjacent side is next to θ. The side facing the right angle is the hypotenuse.
The side facing the right angle is the longest side: the hypotenuse.

practice.question: A right triangle has sides 8, 15 and 17. The angle θ faces the side 8. What is cos θ?
practice.why: cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse. The adjacent side is 15 and the hypotenuse is 17.
wrong: That is sin θ, opposite ÷ hypotenuse. cos uses the adjacent side: 15/17.
That is tan θ, opposite ÷ adjacent. cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse = 15/17.
That is upside down. cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse = 15/17.

practice.question: A right triangle has sides 5, 12 and 13. The angle θ faces the side 12. What is tan θ?
practice.why: The opposite side is 12 and the adjacent side is 5. tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent = 12/5.
wrong: That is for the other sharp angle. From this θ the opposite side is 12: 12/5.
That is sin θ, opposite ÷ hypotenuse. tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent = 12/5.
That is cos θ, adjacent ÷ hypotenuse. tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent = 12/5.

practice.question: A ladder 10 m long leans against a wall. Its foot is 6 m from the wall and its top is 8 m up the wall. θ is the angle between the ladder and the ground. What is sin θ?
practice.why: The wall (8) is opposite θ and the ladder (10) is the hypotenuse. sin θ = 8/10.
wrong: The ground (6) is the adjacent side, so that is cos θ. sin θ = 8/10.
That is tan θ, opposite ÷ adjacent. sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse = 8/10.
That is upside down. sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse = 8/10.

entries.concept: cosec, sec and cot, and what sin²θ means
entries.evidence: The lessons ask 'find cot θ', state 'sec(90° − θ) = cosec θ' and evaluate sin²45° before the reciprocal ratios are defined (only in the next skill) and without saying what the small 2 means.

screens.title: Three more ratios, and sin²θ
text: Turn each of sin, cos and tan upside down and you get three more ratios. cosec θ = hypotenuse ÷ opposite = 1 ÷ sin θ. sec θ = hypotenuse ÷ adjacent = 1 ÷ cos θ. cot θ = adjacent ÷ opposite = 1 ÷ tan θ.
They are read 'cosecant', 'secant' and 'cotangent'. A way to remember the pairs: each pair has exactly one 'co': sin with cosec, cos with sec, tan with cot.
One more piece of writing. sin²θ means (sin θ)², that is sin θ × sin θ. The small 2 is put after 'sin' so that nobody thinks the angle is being squared.
example: Sides 3, 4, 5 with θ facing the side 3: sin θ = 3/5, cos θ = 4/5, tan θ = 3/4
cosec θ = 5/3, sec θ = 5/4, cot θ = 4/3

check.question: tan θ = 2/7. What is cot θ?

practice.question: Which ratio is 1 ÷ cos θ?
practice.why: Each pair has exactly one 'co': cos goes with sec. sec θ = 1 ÷ cos θ.
wrong: cosec θ is 1 ÷ sin θ. cos pairs with sec.
cot θ is 1 ÷ tan θ. cos pairs with sec.
cos²θ is cos θ × cos θ. Turning cos upside down gives sec θ.

practice.question: sin θ = 2/3. What is cosec θ?
practice.why: cosec θ = 1 ÷ sin θ, so turn 2/3 upside down: 3/2.
wrong: That is sin θ again. cosec turns it upside down: 3/2.
That is sin²θ. cosec θ is sin θ turned upside down: 3/2.
Turning upside down does not change the sign. cosec θ = 3/2.

practice.question: sin θ = 1/2. What is sin²θ?
practice.why: sin²θ means sin θ × sin θ = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
wrong: You doubled. sin²θ means sin θ × sin θ = 1/4.
That is 1 ÷ sin θ, which is cosec θ. sin²θ = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
That is still sin θ. The small 2 squares it: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

practice.question: A right triangle has sides 5, 12 and 13. The angle θ faces the side 5. What is sec θ?
practice.why: The adjacent side is 12. sec θ = hypotenuse ÷ adjacent = 13/12.
wrong: That is cosec θ, hypotenuse ÷ opposite. sec uses the adjacent side: 13/12.
That is cos θ. sec θ is cos θ turned upside down: 13/12.
That is cot θ, adjacent ÷ opposite. sec θ = hypotenuse ÷ adjacent = 13/12.

entries.concept: minutes of a degree (46°32′)
entries.evidence: The tables lesson asks for sin 46°32′ and speaks of 'every 6′' without saying that a degree is divided into 60 minutes.

screens.title: Smaller than a degree: minutes
text: One hour is cut into 60 minutes so that we can tell time more exactly. One degree is cut up the same way, for measuring angles more exactly.
1 degree = 60 minutes. A minute of angle is written with a small mark: 60′. So 30′ is half a degree and 6′ is one tenth of a degree.

46°32′ is read '46 degrees 32 minutes'. It is a little more than 46 and a half degrees. Tables list values every 6′ and give a small correction for the 1′ to 5′ in between. For sin and tan the correction is added. For cos it is subtracted, because cos gets smaller as the angle grows.
example: So look in the 46° row under 30′, then use the correction for 2′ (add it for sin and tan, subtract it for cos).

check.question: How many minutes are there in half a degree?

practice.question: How many minutes are there in 1 degree?
practice.why: A degree is cut up like an hour: 1 degree = 60 minutes.
wrong: A degree is not cut into 100. Like an hour, it has 60 minutes.
30′ is half a degree. A whole degree is 60′.
360 is the degrees in a full turn. One degree has 60′.

practice.question: What part of a degree is 15′?
practice.why: 1 degree = 60′, and 15 is one quarter of 60.
wrong: Half a degree is 30′. 15′ is a quarter.
One tenth of a degree is 6′. 15′ is 15/60, a quarter.
Divide by 60, not by 15: 15/60 is one quarter.

practice.question: How do you write 20°30′ in degrees only?
practice.why: 30′ is half a degree, so 20°30′ = 20.5°.
wrong: 30′ is not 0.3 of a degree. 30 out of 60 is a half: 20.5°.
Do not add degrees and minutes. 30′ is half a degree: 20.5°.
30′ is 30/60 of a degree, which is 0.5. So it is 20.5°.

practice.question: Tables list values every 6′ (0′, 6′, 12′, ... 42′, 48′, 54′). How do you look up sin 25°44′?
options: 25° row under 48′, then add the correction for 4′
25° row under 42′, then add the correction for 2′
25° row under 40′, then add the correction for 4′
25° row under 42′, then subtract the correction for 2′
practice.why: 44′ = 42′ + 2′. Use the column 42′ and, for sin, add the correction for 2′.
wrong: Corrections are for the extra minutes above a column. Use the column just below: 42′ + 2′.
There is no 40′ column; columns go in steps of 6′. Use 42′ + 2′.
Subtracting is for cos. For sin the correction is added.

entries.concept: naming a triangle's sides a, b, c opposite the angles A, B, C
entries.evidence: The first lesson is titled 'a/sin A = b/sin B' and its example gives 'A = 30°, B = 45°, a = 2' without saying which side a is.

screens.title: Small letter faces capital letter
text: Until now sin and cos lived in right triangles. The sine rule and cosine rule work in any triangle, so we need a way to name its parts.

Call the corners A, B and C. The same capital letters also stand for the angles at those corners. Each side is named with the small letter of the corner it faces: side a is opposite angle A (it joins B and C), side b is opposite angle B, and side c is opposite angle C.

So a and A never touch: they face each other across the triangle. The bigger an angle, the longer the side facing it. The sine rule says exactly how: a ÷ sin A, b ÷ sin B and c ÷ sin C are all the same number.
example: Triangle ABC with A = 30°, B = 45°, a = 2
a = 2 is the side BC, facing the 30° angle.
b is the side AC, facing the 45° angle. It must be longer than a.
Sine rule: 2 ÷ sin 30° = 2 ÷ 1/2 = 4, so b = 4 × sin 45° = 2√2, about 2.83.

check.question: In triangle ABC, which side is opposite the angle B?
check.answer: Side b (the side joining A and C)

practice.question: In triangle ABC, which angle is the side a opposite to?
practice.why: Each side has the small letter of the corner it faces. Side a faces angle A.
wrong: Side a touches the corner B. It faces the angle A.
Side a touches the corner C. It faces the angle A.
The triangle need not have a right angle. Side a faces angle A.

practice.question: In triangle ABC, which two corners does the side c join?
options: C and the middle of AB
practice.why: Side c faces the corner C, so it joins the other two corners, A and B.
wrong: That is side a, which faces A. Side c never touches C.
That is side b, which faces B. Side c never touches C.
A side joins two corners. Side c faces C and joins A and B.

practice.question: In triangle ABC, A = 50°, B = 100° and C = 30°. Which side is the shortest?
practice.why: The smaller the angle, the shorter the side facing it. The smallest angle is C, so c is shortest.
wrong: a faces the 50° angle. The smallest angle is C = 30°, so c is shortest.
b faces the biggest angle, 100°, so it is the longest side.
Equal sides face equal angles. 50° and 30° differ, and c is shorter.

practice.question: In triangle ABC, A = 30°, B = 90° and a = 5. Use the sine rule to find b. (sin 30° = 1/2, sin 90° = 1)
wrong: b faces the bigger angle, so it must be longer than a. b = 10 × sin 90° = 10.
You multiplied 5 by 1/2. Divide: 5 ÷ 1/2 = 10, then b = 10 × 1 = 10.
You doubled twice. 5 ÷ 1/2 = 10, and b = 10 × sin 90° = 10.

entries.concept: the notation î, ĵ, k̂ and what a position vector is
entries.evidence: The first lesson begins 'Vectors in î, ĵ, k̂ form are added and scaled' and the next uses 'position vectors −6î − k̂' without saying what î, ĵ, k̂ or a position vector is.

screens.title: Three building-block arrows
text: Directions from a street corner sound like '2 blocks east, then 3 blocks north'. You build any trip out of steps in a few fixed directions.

For vectors the fixed steps are î, ĵ and k̂. î is the unit vector along the x-axis, ĵ along the y-axis and k̂ along the z-axis. The hat on top says the length is 1. In components, î = (1, 0, 0), ĵ = (0, 1, 0) and k̂ = (0, 0, 1).
Every vector is so many î plus so many ĵ plus so many k̂. So 2î + 3ĵ − k̂ is the same vector as (2, 3, −1). A missing letter means that component is 0: 4î + 2ĵ = (4, 2, 0).
The position vector of a point P is the arrow from the origin O to P, written OP. Its components are simply the coordinates of P.
example: P is (3, −1, 2). Its position vector is 3î − ĵ + 2k̂.

check.question: Write 5î − 2ĵ + k̂ as components (x, y, z).

practice.question: Along which axis does the unit vector î point?
practice.why: î is the unit vector along the x-axis: (1, 0, 0).
wrong: The y-axis has ĵ. î points along the x-axis.
The z-axis has k̂. î points along the x-axis.
The arrow from O to P is the position vector. î is fixed along the x-axis.

practice.question: Write the vector (2, −5, 4) using î, ĵ and k̂.
practice.why: The components go in order: 2 with î, −5 with ĵ, 4 with k̂.
wrong: The sign of −5 was lost. The ĵ part is −5ĵ.
The first two are swapped. x goes with î and y with ĵ.
x and z are swapped. The first component 2 goes with î.

practice.question: Write 3î + 7k̂ as components (x, y, z).
practice.why: ĵ is missing, so the y-component is 0. k̂ gives the z-component 7.
wrong: 7 goes with k̂, the z-axis. The missing ĵ gives y = 0.
A missing letter means 0, not nothing. Write all three: (3, 0, 7).
3 goes with î, the x-axis. It is ĵ that is missing: (3, 0, 7).

practice.question: A is (2, 1, 3) and B is (5, 1, 4). What is the vector AB?
wrong: You added the coordinates. AB = OB − OA = (3, 0, 1).
That is OA − OB, the vector from B to A. AB = OB − OA.
The y-parts are 1 − 1 = 0, so there is no ĵ term.

entries.concept: what adding vectors and multiplying a vector by a number mean
entries.evidence: The lesson says vectors 'are added and scaled component by component' and asks for 3a − 3b, but never says what the sum of two vectors or a multiple of a vector is as an arrow.

screens.title: Adding arrows, stretching arrows
text: Walk 3 east and 1 north. Then walk 1 east and 2 north. Altogether you have gone 4 east and 3 north. That is vector addition: follow the first arrow, then the second one from where the first ended. The sum is the single arrow from the start to the finish.
This is why vectors are added component by component: the easts add up, and the norths add up.

Multiplying a vector by a number stretches it. 2a is twice as long as a in the same direction. −a has the same length and the opposite direction. Every component is multiplied by the number. The number is called a scalar.
A mixture such as 3a − 2b is called a linear combination of a and b.

check.question: a = (1, 2, 3). What is 2a?

practice.question: What is the number that multiplies a vector called?
practice.why: The number that stretches a vector is called a scalar.
wrong: A unit vector is a vector of length 1. The multiplying number is a scalar.
Components are the parts of the vector. The multiplying number is a scalar.
That is a mixture such as 3a − 2b. The number alone is a scalar.

practice.question: a = (2, 5, 1) and b = (4, 1, 3). What is a + b?
practice.why: Add component by component: (2 + 4, 5 + 1, 1 + 3) = (6, 6, 4).
wrong: You multiplied the components. Adding gives (6, 6, 4).
You subtracted b. Adding gives (6, 6, 4).
A sum of vectors is a vector. Keep the components apart: (6, 6, 4).

practice.question: a = (1, −3, 2). What is −2a?
practice.why: Multiply every component by −2: −2 × 1 = −2, −2 × −3 = 6, −2 × 2 = −4.
wrong: Only the first component was multiplied. Every component is multiplied by −2.
−2 × −3 is +6, not −6. Minus times minus gives plus.
You added −2 to each component. Multiply instead: (−2, 6, −4).

practice.question: You walk 2 east and 5 north. Then you walk 3 west and 1 north. Where are you from the start? (West counts as minus east.)
practice.why: East: 2 − 3 = −1, that is 1 west. North: 5 + 1 = 6.
wrong: West is the opposite of east, so subtract: 2 − 3 = −1, that is 1 west.
2 − 3 = −1. The minus sign means west, not east.
Both walks go north, so add: 5 + 1 = 6 north.

entries.concept: what a vector is: size and direction, components, the vector from A to B, magnitude, unit vector
entries.evidence: The first vectors lesson says direction cosines 'are the components of the unit vector' and works with 'the vector AB' and |AB|, but no earlier lesson says what a vector, a component or a unit vector is.

screens.title: An arrow: how far and which way
text: 'Walk 5 km' does not say where you end up. 'Walk 5 km north-east' does. Some quantities need a direction as well as a size.

A quantity with a size and a direction is called a vector. We draw it as an arrow: its length shows the size and it points in the direction. A movement from one place to another, a velocity and a force are vectors. A quantity with only a size, such as mass or time, is called a scalar.
The vector that takes you from point A to point B is written AB with an arrow on top. Two arrows with the same length and the same direction are the same vector, wherever they are drawn.
example: Walk 3 km east, then 4 km north.
You are now 3 east and 4 north of the start.
Your whole movement is one arrow, 5 km long, from start to finish.

check.question: Is temperature a vector or a scalar?
check.answer: A scalar: it has a size but no direction

screens.title: A vector as three numbers
text: On a grid, a vector is described by how far it goes along each axis. These numbers are its components. The vector (2, 1, 2) goes 2 along x, 1 along y and 2 along z.
To get the vector from A to B, subtract the coordinates of A from those of B: end minus start. In short, AB = B − A.
The length of a vector is called its magnitude and is written with bars, |AB|. By Pythagoras, used twice, it is √(x² + y² + z²), where x, y and z are the components.

check.question: A is (0, 0, 0) and B is (1, 2, 2). What is |AB|?

screens.title: Unit vectors and direction cosines
text: A unit vector is a vector of length exactly 1. It keeps the direction and throws away the size. To make one, divide every component of a vector by its length.

The components of a unit vector have a meaning. Take the angle between the vector and the x-axis. In the right triangle with the vector as hypotenuse, the x-component is the adjacent side. So the cosine of that angle is (x-component) ÷ (length). The same holds for the y-axis and the z-axis.
These three cosines are called the direction cosines, written l, m, n. The undivided components, or any multiple of them, are called direction ratios.

check.question: What is the length of a unit vector?

practice.question: Which of these is a vector?
options: A wind blowing at 20 km/h towards the east
practice.why: It has a size (20 km/h) and a direction (east), so it is a vector.
wrong: Mass has a size but no direction. It is a scalar.
Time has a size but no direction. It is a scalar.
Temperature has a size but no direction. It is a scalar.

practice.question: A is (2, 0, 1) and B is (5, 4, 1). What is the vector AB?
wrong: That is start minus end, A − B. AB = B − A = (3, 4, 0).
You added the coordinates. Subtract: B − A = (3, 4, 0).
The z-part must be subtracted too: 1 − 1 = 0.

practice.question: What is the magnitude of the vector (2, 3, 6)?
wrong: You added the components. Square them, add, then take the root: √49 = 7.
49 is the sum of the squares. Take its square root: 7.
6 is only the biggest component. The length is √(4 + 9 + 36) = 7.

practice.question: What is the unit vector in the direction of (0, 3, 4)?
practice.why: The length is √(0 + 9 + 16) = 5. Divide every component by 5.
wrong: Its length is 5, not 1. Divide every component by 5.
That changes the direction, and its length is √2. Divide by the length 5 instead.
You divided by 3 + 4. Divide by the length √(9 + 16) = 5.

entries.concept: the two ways to multiply vectors: the dot product gives a number, the cross product gives a vector (right-hand rule)
entries.evidence: The lesson opens with the formulas 'a · b = |a| |b| cos θ, and a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃' and later 'a × b ... (right-hand rule)' without saying what kind of thing each product is, what it measures or what the right-hand rule is.

screens.title: The dot product: one number from two arrows
text: Pull a trolley with a rope held at a slant. Only the part of your pull that points along the floor moves the trolley. The dot product measures this: how much one vector acts along another.

The dot product a · b is a number, not a vector. It equals |a| × |b| × cos θ, where θ is the angle between the two arrows. If they point the same way, cos θ = 1 and the dot product is as big as it can be. If they are at right angles, cos 90° = 0, so the dot product is 0. If the angle is more than 90°, it is negative.
There is an easy way to work it out: multiply the matching components and add. Having two ways to get the same number is what lets us find the angle.

check.question: a = (1, 0, 0) and b = (0, 1, 0). What is a · b?
check.answer: 0, because the two vectors are at right angles

screens.title: The cross product: a new arrow at right angles
text: Turn a screw with a spanner. You push sideways on the handle, yet the screw moves along its own length, at right angles to both the handle and your push. The cross product describes this kind of situation.
The cross product a × b is a vector. It is at right angles to both a and b. Its length is |a| × |b| × sin θ, which is the area of the parallelogram with sides a and b.

There are two opposite directions at right angles to both arrows. The right-hand rule picks one: point the fingers of your right hand along a and curl them towards b. Your thumb shows the direction of a × b. So b × a points the opposite way. The order matters.
example: It points along the z-axis, at right angles to both.
Its length 6 is the area of the 2 by 3 rectangle on a and b.

check.question: Is a × b a number or a vector?

practice.question: What kind of thing is the dot product a · b?
options: A vector at right angles to a and b
practice.why: The dot product is a number, not a vector.
wrong: That describes the cross product a × b. The dot product is a number.
The dot product is not a vector at all. It is one number.
It helps to find the angle, but a · b itself is a number: |a| × |b| × cos θ.

practice.question: a = (1, 2, 3) and b = (4, 0, 1). What is a · b?
practice.why: Multiply the matching components and add: 1 × 4 + 2 × 0 + 3 × 1 = 7.
wrong: You multiplied but did not add. The dot product is one number: 4 + 0 + 3 = 7.
You added all the components. Multiply matching ones first: 4 + 0 + 3 = 7.
One zero component does not make the whole product 0. 4 + 0 + 3 = 7.

practice.question: a × b = (0, 0, 5). What is b × a?
practice.why: The order matters: b × a points the opposite way to a × b.
wrong: Swapping the order reverses the direction. b × a = (0, 0, −5).
The cross product is a vector and does not vanish on swapping. It only reverses.
Swapping does not move it to another axis. It only reverses: (0, 0, −5).

practice.question: Two vectors a and b have lengths 2 and 5 and are at right angles. Which is right? (cos 90° = 0, sin 90° = 1)
options: a · b = 10 and the length of a × b is 0
a · b = 10 and the length of a × b is 10
a · b = 0 and the length of a × b is 10
a · b = 0 and the length of a × b is 0
practice.why: a · b = 2 × 5 × cos 90° = 0. The length of a × b is 2 × 5 × sin 90° = 10.
wrong: These are swapped. The dot product uses cos 90° = 0; the cross product uses sin 90° = 1.
The dot product uses cos θ, and cos 90° = 0. So a · b = 0.
The cross product uses sin θ, and sin 90° = 1. Its length is 2 × 5 = 10.

entries.concept: what a parallelepiped is, and why a · (b × c) is its volume
entries.evidence: The first lesson says the size of [a b c] 'is the volume of the parallelepiped on a, b, c' and no lesson says what a parallelepiped is.

screens.title: A leaning box
text: Take a neat stack of books and push the top sideways so that the stack leans. Its sides are now slanted parallelograms. A solid whose six faces are all parallelograms is called a parallelepiped. A cuboid is the special case that stands upright.
Such a box is fixed by the three edges that leave one corner. Call them the vectors a, b and c. Its volume is base area × height.

The number a · (b × c) gives exactly this. The length of b × c is the area of the base on b and c, and dotting with a picks out the height. This number is called the scalar triple product and is written [a b c]. It can come out negative, so the volume is its size, |[a b c]|.
If a, b and c all lie flat in one plane, the box has no height and the volume is 0. Such vectors are called coplanar.

check.question: A box has edges 1, 2 and 5 that meet at right angles. What is its volume?

practice.question: What is a solid called whose six faces are all parallelograms?
practice.why: A solid with six parallelogram faces is a parallelepiped, like a leaning box.
wrong: A parallelogram is a flat shape, one face. The solid is a parallelepiped.
That is the number a · (b × c) giving the volume. The solid is a parallelepiped.
Coplanar describes vectors lying in one plane. The solid is a parallelepiped.

practice.question: a = (2, 0, 0), b = (0, 2, 0) and c = (0, 0, 3). What is a · (b × c)?
practice.why: b × c = (6, 0, 0), and a · (6, 0, 0) = 2 × 6 = 12. Check: an upright 2 by 2 by 3 box.
wrong: You added the edge lengths. Volume multiplies: 2 × 2 × 3 = 12.
That is only b × c, a vector. Dot it with a to get the number 12.
It is 0 only when the three vectors lie in one plane. Here they do not: it is 12.

practice.question: For three edge vectors, [a b c] = −12. What is the volume of the box?
practice.why: The volume is the size of the triple product: |−12| = 12.
wrong: A volume cannot be negative. Take the size: 12.
The volume is 0 only when [a b c] = 0. Here it is |−12| = 12.
Do not square to remove the sign. Just take the size: 12.

practice.question: Three pencils lie flat on a table with their ends at one point. Taken as vectors a, b and c, what is a · (b × c)?
practice.why: All three lie in one plane, so the box has no height and its volume is 0.
wrong: A flat box has no height, so its volume is 0, not 1.
That is only for edges at right angles. Flat vectors give no height: 0.
The triple product is a volume, and a flat box has none: 0.
